title: Survive DnD-style wizarding school shenanigans in this TTRPG
content:
Dungeons and Dragons built itself upon a foundation of swords and sorcery.  These days, It's reached a point that players of the swords persuasion feel that sorcery gets more toys to play around with. Regardless of balance, that's simply the situation when sorcery lets you bend reality to your whim. Yet most casters don't get to that "whim" part so easy. They need training and guidance.

Some sort of wizarding school, one could say.

Academia Arcana RPG is an upcoming fantasy RPG set in the Eternal Academy, a wizard school full of mysteries from eons of magical learning. The game features over 200 pages that detail the classes, spells, and denizens you will meet on this wizarding adventure. Naturally, those of the sorcery persuasion with their DnD classes will have an easier time acclimating to the curriculum.

It runs on the Dungeon Crawl Classics system, an OSR-infused take on DnD-style gameplay. As expected of an OSR game, dangerous situations are short and lethal. The perfect adjectives to use for reliving high school when the kids have access to Fireball. Adding to the danger of other teenagers are various monsters, ranging from familiar DnD races to the more esoteric spawn you'd expect from a wizarding school.

It's such fun having a staple trope of my childhood come to the tabletop with this much love poured into it. Kids and YA books especially loved the concept, special places where young people could unlock their hidden potential. What makes these so exciting is the very real dangers they face, balancing out the fun with surprising tension.  Magic is dangerous, yet at the same time, it is so intoxicating in its appeal.

The gorgeous art style does a fantastic job of portraying that. These covers in particular show a great range of magical experiences. A study session where you slowly become embraced by the spells, a volatile incantation hot to the touch, pure whimsy at learning something beautiful, and sinister concoctions requiring a delicate touch. Needless to say, I'm very excited for the final release.

You can check out Academia Arcana RPG on Backerkit here!

For more magical experiences, the Wargamer Discord has plenty of wizards, though we can't promise they're all of the coast.

title: The latest Warhammer 40k previews are green and very, very mean
content:
Warhammer 40k is about to take further steps into the new edition thanks to the upcoming slate of Ork releases. Featured in a recent official preview, the new Codex for the Orks alongside Nazdreg (the notorious Bad Moon warlord), the Warboss kit, Mek box, Boyz squad and a range of vehicles will soon go up for pre-order. If tradition is any indicator, these sets will likely go up for pre-order on August 22, alongside numerous solo releases from the Ork side of the Armageddon box set. 

At the top of the new Warhammer Community preview is Codex: Orks, the first faction book for the new edition of Warhammer 40k. As you'd expect from a Codex, it boasts plenty of lore and new rules, including 15 new detachments and datasheets for the over 50 units that make up the faction. It also includes codes for the Warhammer 40k App, if you're into that sort of thing. 

As is typical across all 40k faction updates, there's also a Collector's Edition for the codex, complete with a fancy cover and gilded page edges. 

The preview features plenty of Ork models, including the power-armored menace that is Nazdreg as well as a heavily customizable Warboss kit. Much to my enjoyment, the kit includes an attack squig as well as a range of different base and weapon options; we love to see it. 

The new Mek kit is also here, complete with a shoulder-mounted crane and a grim scowl, while the Boyz kit offers a welcome reinvention of the classic core unit. For fans of going fast, we've got the Trukk and the Warbikers. The Warbikers are a particular gem, their sculpts capturing a real sense of motion.

Lastly, we have a range of kits up for preview previously only available through the Armageddon box set. These include the Big Mek Dakkarig, the Weirdboy, the Wartrakk, and a Kommand Krew composed of a Bannernob, Bigboss and Painboy.

title: This solo samurai TTRPG tells a story through stones in real life
content:
Tabletop RPGs have an underrated advantage versus other forms of gaming art: reality. While these games will always require some level of imagination, the experience itself requires real elements that the player directly interacts with. The roll of a dice, the presence of other players, hardbound books containing loads of lore, all of it a series of haptic feedbacks for your experience. I'm always fascinated when a TTRPG takes full advantage of the fact that it's in the real world to tell a story.

This samurai RPG approaches that in an incredibly innovative way.

Samurai: Five Stones by Pinayu is a solo journaling TTRPG wherein the player builds the story of a samurai through five stones. You can acquire these stones from anywhere in the world. Cracked pieces of concrete crag, mossy stones damp with lakeside wet, and smooth obsidian glistening in the dark tell the tale of your samurai. Instead of DnD classes, the stones as you build the story, noting down characteristics such as shape, color and texture.

The sampler page gives us a good idea of how this runs. Outside my house, I looked around for some choice looking stones for the first part of our story: a rivalry. I found a medium-sized slab, light gray and oval, its surface eroded by the elements. This meant the samurai confronted Tomoe, a student from the same dojo who stuns with beauty and swiftness. By the riverside, my samurai clashes with Tomoe, but they are too evenly matched. Unbeknownst to both, a mysterious observer saw it all happen.

I don't know about you, but this doesn't take too much modifying to become an enemies-to-lovers story (bonus points for queer love). All that from a rock, which in-universe of your story, existed in that space. And with more rocks than there are DnD races, you're bound to craft a unique story.

You can check out Samurai: Five Stones on itch.io here!

title: The Pokémon TCG's Darkrai SIR is worth almost $100 less now than when Pitch Black launched
content:
We once described Mega Darkrai EX as the most metal Pokémon card, and it does a pretty great job of getting across the grimdark vibes of the Pitch Black expansion. This nightmarish card has taken a bit of a tumble in price, though, dropping from being worth roughly $300 (£221) to roughly $200 ($147). Let's take a look at what happened to the price of the edgiest Pokémon card.

According to price data from TCGplayer, a near mint copy of the SIR Darkrai was worth $301(£222) on the 18th July, the day after the release of Pitch Black. The card is currently worth $208 (£153), a fall of 31%. Darkrai is still definitely pricey, but it's a far less expensive Pokémon card than it was before.

So, what's behind this price climbdown? As with any story related to TCG finances, there are no unambiguous answers, and it's impossible to say without indulging in at least a little bit of speculation. With that said, this does follow a general pattern where exciting new chase cards gradually decline in value, as the expansion that introduced them becomes increasingly available. Both Chaos Rising and Perfect Order saw similar results, as the SIR versions of Mega Greninja and Mega Zygarde from those sets lost value over time in the months after they were released.

Additionally, the Pokémon TCG's upcoming 30th Celebration expansion is generating an incredible amount of hype. This is swallowing up a lot of focus which would otherwise have been directed towards Pitch Black. Because of this, the attention of the Pokémon TCG community is directed firmly towards the future, leaving this twisted and brooding dark type to the wayside as an exciting anniversary party approaches.

Do you prefer Pokémon cards that are dark, gripping, and edgy, or cards that are colorful, cute, and playful? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord.

title: More than 10% of the wolves in MTG were introduced in The Hobbit
content:
Inside you there are two wolves, and statistically they each have an 11.9% chance of coming from MTG's The Hobbit expansion. That's right, over the course of Magic: the Gathering's 33 year long history, 101 wolves have been printed. 12 of these lupine trading cards are brand new additions released in The Hobbit, or one of the supplemental products brought out alongside it.

Why are so many wolves roaming Middle-Earth now when there were barely any included in the previous Lord of the Rings expansion? Well, Wargs, a Tolkienian species of evil wolves, were one of the five belligerents that fought in the Battle of Five Armies. This climactic clash occurred towards the end of The Hobbit book, and throughout the third Peter Jackson film.

Out of all the MTG sets in the game's history, The Hobbit is the first to make Wolf typal its own supported theme, without sharing the focus with werewolves. The green and black archetype featured in The Hobbit drafts is based on wolves and utilizes the ferocious mechanic. Players are encouraged to gather together a pack that can buff each other up, and provide beneficial effects while you control a creature with power four or greater.

Wolves have also gotten a new typal commander in the form of Chief of the Wilds. This silver coated 4/4 gains two +1/+1 counters whenever you play another wolf, and it causes the triggered abilities of your wolves and battles to activate an additional time. At the moment, Chief of the Wilds is only available as a borderless card inside Collector Boosters. During 2027, though, the Battle of the Five Armies Co-op Kit will drop, and make this warg warlord more widely available.

Are you looking to rustle up some wolves, or have other cards from The Hobbit caught your eye? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord.

title: The Ogor Mawtribes' roster of gorgeous new Warhammer minis is now available for pre-order
content:
Warhammer: Age of Sigmar is rightly renowned for offering a wide range of larger-than-life armies. However, it's the Ogor Mawtribes who, perhaps, account for the most oversized of all. The entire faction consists of hulking brutes three times the size of a mortal human, each possessed of ravenous, destructive appetites. This distinctive faction is getting a brand new range of models which, I'm pleased to report, is now up for pre-order. 

Though some of the offerings in Games Workshop's latest pre-order post were available in the Ogor Mawtribes Army Set, this is the first time that the Age of Sigmar faction's full roster has been available for purchase. This includes Morga The Mighty, a new named character for the Ogor Mawtribes who rides into battle on a mighty Glutthorn. If you're looking to make a warlord of your own, however, the kit can also be assembled as an unnamed Tyrant. Redd the Maw, the cauldron-toting High Slaughtermaster, and Grell Firefist, a grizzled cannoneer, are also available. 

Kits for Tyrants and Butchers are also up for grabs, alongside boxes for the elite Ironguts and the hulking Gluttons, which make up the bulk of any Ogor Mawtribes army. Those looking for more spiritually inclined brutes can find what they're looking for in the Cleavers kit (which can also be assembled as Gutseers, if you're a fan of hooded zealots). 

Ogors are also well known for their array of monstrous mounts and beastly allies. Maulbeast Raiders (also buildable as Maulbeast Cavalry) provided a rapid, flanking option for prospective warlords, while Hunters with Sabrefangs and Mantrappers provide valuable disruption. If you're looking for something more exotic, Okar's Torrbad is a regiment of renown which includes two Ogors on a pair of massive monstrous mounts. 

The new Ogor Mawtribes Battletome is also available in both standard and Gamer's editions, alongside some snazzy Mawtribes-themed dice. 

It's a rare joy to see a faction rejuvenated so completely. I can't wait to see the way the folks at my local games store paint up these gorgeous new sculpts.

title: I hope that the Pokémon TCG's 30th Celebration set remembers to show Raichu some love
content:
Pikachu is probably the most famous mascot in the world. There are people out there who have never picked up a Pokémon card or played a Pokémon game who can still absolutely identify the electric mouse on sight because the character is just that ubiquitous. Because of this, Pikachu is featured on more than 230 Pokéon cards. Its evolved form Raichu is not so lucky, appearing on less than 60 cards and often gettting outshone by its more famous predecessor.

The upcoming 30th Celebration Pokémon TCG set includes a collection of 30 special anniversary Pikachu cards drawn by some of the game's most beloved artists. It also features two distinct Pikachu ex cards and a reprint of the shocking powerhouse Pikachu and Zekrom GX. Meanwhile, it hasn't yet been officially confirmed whether a Raichu card will even be making an appearance in the set.

This isn't to say Raichu has gotten no love over the course of the TCG's history. One of the rarest Pokémon cards out there is actually a Raichu, but it certainly gets less time in the spotlight compared to its smaller, cuter counterpart.

At least Raichu has gotten more representation than Pichu (the first stage of the evolution line), who has currently only appeared on 20 Pokémon cards. Then again, despite being a baby, Pichu is a playable character in Super Smash Brothers, while Raichu is not. This means that the big orange bolt slinger will tragically never get the chance to hang out with Chrom from Fire Emblem.

We've not seen all of the spoilers for the 30th Celebration set yet, so it's possible that the Pokémon Company are just holding Raichu in reserve. Personally, I really hope to see the entire evolution line making an appearance, ideally teamed up together in some adorable Illustration Rare artwork.

title: The secret to success in MTG's newest limited format is… pinecones?
content:
The Hobbit officially released this Friday, and MTG players are busy figuring out the quirks of the game's latest limited format. While it's still incredibly early in The Hobbit's lifespan, and the set is far from 'solved', reliable and versatile cards are often identified during these initial stages of play through experimentation and speculation. Let's talk about Pinecone Strike, and why this arboreal attack seems to be generating so much attention.

To win any game of Limited in MTG, you need to ensure that you have a reliable suite of removal spells, and every color deals with threats slightly differently. Red is famous for blowing up its problems through direct damage. Because of this, almost All MTG Sets feature a two mana spell that deals three damage, or a close equivalent. Pinecone Strike fills this niche for The Hobbit, but some quirks about its effect, as well as about the format more broadly, make it one of the most desirable common cards in the set.

When cast, Pinecone Strike deals three damage to a creature, and then exiles them if it would destroy them. In addition to that, it can also destroy an artifact token controlled by the opponent. Notably, you can activate both of these modes, you don't have to choose one or the other. This means that you can take out an opponent's Ravening Warg at the same time as destroying one of their treasure tokens.

Ben Werne, one of the hosts of the Lords of Limited podcast, describes Pinecone Strike as "broken" thanks to The Hobbit containing a "plethora of X/2" creatures ready for it to take out. Marshall Sutcliffe, from Limited Resources, states that it is "great, obviously".

Is Pinecone Strike going to break into constructed any time soon? Probably not, but in the specific self-contained world of The Hobbit drafts, these pinecones can really pull their weight.

Thoughts

T'au as an army are tailor-made for Purge the Foe and this list plays directly into the army's strengths, running units which can hit hard and move quickly. The biggest challenge for Retaliation Cadre lists is weapon teching for the current meta: Starscythe units with Burst Cannons are great into Ork hordes but nearly worthless into big knights, and the natural advantage of Purge vs. Take and Hold - that you score for killing while your opponent has to bring units to the middle of the table to get killed - is mitigated by playing into a list of big knights, where all your energy has to be spent taking down massive threats. Those threats also double as having a lot of OC, making it easy for them to sit and hold objectives. T'au lists don't love punching up, but can usually make up for having to roll 5+ to wound by throwing out a ton of volume with high-damage shots. But a few choice 5+ invulnerable saves from the knights can make that all moot - a single knight living on 1 wound can easily decide a game, and that Knight Lancer's small number of attacks plays very well into targets like Crisis Suits and the Ghostkeel.

The plan for the knights player here is to just dominate the board's central objectives, pushing forward with the Lancer while the Atropos, Canis, and Crusader hang back and hold objectives. The Knights player will want to close the gap early - even losing two or three units can make a huge difference in the matchup, as the T'au player needs to combine shooting from the Hammerhead, Ghostkeel, and Broadsides to make something happen.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews- Ogor Mawtribes Gutbusters and Beastclaw Raiders
content:
Alrighty Ogor Fans! A few weeks ago we devoured the new Ogor Mawtribes Army Box and now we’re back with the second course of tasty gristle and throbbing meat. Games Workshop were extremely generous with their portions of review models for us to gobble up! So the team has been working hard on building and painting all these new culinary delights to report back to you here. Let's tuck in!

Ogor Mawtribes.
Warhammer Community

What's New

  • Morga the Mighty/Tyrant on Glutthorn (Multi-build kit, Hero or Unique hero, 120mm Oval)
  • Grell Firefist (Unique Hero, 50mm base)
  • 5 Hunters with Sabrefangs (40mm and 60mm oval bases)

For all the hotness in the Mawseekers go HERE.

Morga the Mighty/Tyrant on Glutthorn

Theresa:

Building

Building Morga the Mighty was a seemingly small task: There were a surprisingly few amount of sprues for such a large lady! Most of the bits fit together well, yet some seams were impossible to hide without sprue goo, especially when they were running down the front of the face of Grutta, her mount. One of my biggest gripes of the kit was where Morga herself sits on the back of Grutta, with the knees-down portion of Morga's legs attaching to Grutta's mount. At this junction, the pieces seemingly can't be put together without a massive gap above the knee. Thankfully, the gap isn't terribly noticeable, but some green stuff to fill the gap would go a long way! The kit is super easy to sub-assemble. I kept Morga separate, as well as the totem pole to airbrush separately. There aren't a ton of options for the model, but if you're building the generic Tyrant the rider is significantly different. It would be easy enough to magnetize the rider to swap between Morga and the Tyrant, though. If you decide to put LEDs in Grutta's eyes (why would anyone ever do that, definitely not something I'm looking to do), the head is assembled to make your life a million times easier, and the torso is hollow!

Painting

I'd like to talk about the textures on this model. She's a giant blank canvas, with a bunch of lovely crackle texture, but there are so many surfaces to have fun with!! The metals have enough layers to make them interesting and pop against the model. I honestly think Grutta looks a bit naked without the thigh panels, but you could absolutely do some fun freehand on her rough skin to make it pop. Morga has a good amount of fun fabrics and textures on her, with teeny details like a pinky ring! She's a little small for the base, so I recommend building up the base with some rocks or foliage to really show off how cute she is.
Morga Credit: Theresa (Mawqueen Minis) Badusernametag: Morga is a cunning and thoughtful general indeed, observing the battlefield with a wry smile that tells of the tactical mind beneeath the embellished helmet.

The other option you can make from this box is a Tyrant on Glutthorn, or GLUTTRANT! the new generic mounted Tyrant for Gutbusters. This big-boned hero is a little more bombastic than his Overtyrant, with slashing choppa raised high and below issuing from maw.

You get alternate:

  • Rider (duh), who has bare head and helmeted options.
  • Back icon-mount, trophy rack thing
  • Head for the Glutthorn

As I’ve alluded above, the Gluttrant is less subtle but maybe a little more dynamic than Morga, and his Glutthorn is also angrier. Big mouth open, teeth on display. His weapon is a little generic, being honest and doesn’t have the impressive heft or savage look of those the foot Tyrant can wield. I think Morga is much cooler, but the monster head here is better, much more interesting. My main criticism of this model generally is that the big cow isn’t very menacing or impressive really. Whilst the skin is sculpted really nicely, I’m not terrified by the whole ‘docile rhino’ vibe. It’s a shame the reins are tied to the rider’s torso build, as Morga riding the more aggro Glutthorn would be nice. I feel like this is a bit of a miss in terms of a Monster mount; unlike the Maulbeast, which are mean looking, demonstrably new and a ‘fantasy’ beast, the Glutthorn is a little too ‘real’ for me. Could it have had six legs? An enormous maw? It just needs something to make it stand out, its enemies fear it and Ogors go WOW!

This kit is pretty cool for bits, which ever version you make. The whole body and arms of each build are unique, so whilst you don’t get more rider legs, you get the whole torso, arms, head (rider) and head of the Glutthorn. I for one am excited to see what a Stornehorn looks like with a Glutthorn head. This could be an easy way to make this kit stretch to TWO Gluttrants? OR just make a fancy ass Forstlord for your new Mawtribe?

I’m excited to play with this kit, but mainly for kitbashing purposes. I’ve got aspirations of leading a mighty horde of Monstrous beasts, and with these two fine riders I may have just found the bits I need and conversion impetuous to make it happen. Watch this space…

GLUTTRANT!!!
Warhammer Community

Grell Firefist

YAARRR!!!

Grell Firefist- Unique Maneater Hero- SPRUE

RIP Leadbelchers, long live Grell Firefist; wandering Ogor Maneater Pirate Captain and badass of the Mawtribe seas! This is the last of the three new Unique Heroes added to the new range, and this time we have a support foot hero with a massive mortar.

It is a little odd that they drop the cannon unit (Leadbelchers) and the Mercenary unit (Maneaters) just as they introduce a unique Hero that is both, but I am not going to argue! There is cannon (pun intended) reasons for this, as the fanatic Redd the Maw convinces the meatiest to give up blackpowder for his support. Sure. This is a great model and a nice concept for what amounts to a special character Tyrant. Here we continue the strong Ogor tradition of Guns (and cannons) for hire! Roaming the realms in search of good scraps, exotic foods and plenty of booty! As someone with a full mercenary blackpowder company I am not sad to add her to my collection.

This model comes on the stock 50mm base you get with big heroes, but unlike the Tyrant, she is actually quite diminutive. Not bigger than a Cleaver, certainly. What Grell lacks in stature she makes up in Firepower however, as that mortar is certainly girthy! 

Grell Firefist- Unique Maneater Hero
Credit: @badusernametag

This is a fun and easy build; no options, but goes together smoothly. Grell has an interesting and quite thoughtful pose for an Ogor; she is looking down at her cannon and has her hand at her side. This is fine, but I think I like something a little more dynamic and aggressive in my fantasy pirate weirdos.

I ended up taking off the stock head and giving her a thick-necked head from the Cleavers kit; added in a knife wielding arm also and I’m happier. Can’t wait to get her painted now and add her to the throng! She will have very grey skin, like my other cave dwellers.

Grell Firefist.
Credit: @badusernametag

Hunters with Sabrefangs

Beastclaw Hunters and Sabrefangs.
Credit: @badusernametag

You get crossbow, they get crossbow, EVERYBODY get crossbow?!

The Beastclaw Raiders have had a smallest portion of the feast in this new range refresh, but that isn’t to say they have been cut out of the pie altogether. By some logic, fighting infantry being covered by the Gutbusters (and now Mawseekers) and having plenty of Monster units, someone at GW decided that the Beastclaw Raiders needed a speciality in ranged units, specifically those with crossbows! The Bloodpelt Hunter shifted over to the Beastclaw sub-faction and gives a nice little boost to all the crossbow toting, infiltrating hunters in the army. I really like the fluff of the big, brutal Ogres also being capable of stealth, that they know the land and stalk prey. It’s nice bit of development that takes us beyond the basics of a brutal and terrifying Ogor horde, only bent on destruction and feasting. So in the new cannon of the Mawtribes the Beastclaw are the subtle ones, attuned with the winter and wild places and on the hunt…

The unit is made up of three Ogor Hunters with crossbows and javelins, and two Sabrefangs. The Sabrefang is a reimagining of the various hunting cats that have accompanied the Beastclaw since the World that Was. Back with a modern kit and a new look.

Beastclaw Hunters and Sabrefangs- Sprue

This is a really great kit with some top notch bits. All the new Ogor kits have some high end food and feasting bits, but these are probs my faves of the bunch. Aside from the cool leather gorget they’re wearing, the Blood Vulture eating from the champions hand and the brutal weapons they’re all carrying theres some stand out snack options I need to highlight.

The first is this gruesome Severed trolls head! Complete with horrified death grimace, this is just casually hung from a Hunters belt, one assumes for a snack later!? Baller.

trolls head!?

The second is this MASSIVE rack of ribs (Carnavlax?) that the other goon is dragging for later. Really great bit.

Amazing bits! Rack of ribs!!!

The Champion is just SO COOL and I am totally enraptured with this bad ass Ogor huntress. So many nice details on her face/head, Blood Vulture, weapons etc. This is my fave of the new range and I just loved every moment of building and painting it!

These models are the usual amazing CAD designed multi-part plastics we are all now privileged to be used to. They go together nicely, often the outer bit of the body forming an interlocking shell that works just so. This does have the advantage for making really beautiful, dynamic models, with very few visible joins or seams. The downsides can be that some joins are fiddly and not obvious to find (instructions help) and that customisation requires you to fully assemble the thing and then hack it up to do a conversion. It’s not like you can take the head, arms etc from one model and easily move to another, as the joins are all unique to each model.

In this instance, one of these is a bit of a fiddle. The one with the crossbow slung over their shoulder has some bits that don’t seem to go instinctively where they should. In all cases such as this I recommend prepping ALL the bits for the model, cleaning the mould lines etc (I use 400 git sand paper to clean all mould lines and joins) and then laying them out in order before starting. This means once you’ve started you can get them all in, before the joins dry. I find that you need to get all of the “shell” together in one go, else you get misalignment.

The crossbow over shoulder guy gets weird on the right hand side, when you get to getting the sword arm on. Take your time and it’s fine.

Hunters- Tricky bit!
Credit: @badusernametag

So here you have an option of BloodVulture or not (spear instead) on the champion and hats or no hats on each model. This isn’t enough variance for me on a unit that you might well want two of. This was true of the Ironguts and it’s a design decision that I’m not really impressed by. These are units I want to repeat without having to make onerous conversions if I don’t want to.

The Sabrefangs are a bit of a ‘meh’ to me. They’re very big plain cats in three parts each. They go together nicely enough and if you’re into sabretoothed tigers sure. But are these especially High Fantasy or AoS? Not really. I know the Ogor Mawtribes are the ‘serious’ Destruction faction, but these don’t do it for me. Could Ogres not hunt with giant mountain worms, toads, or some other unique and interesting beast!? 

In all these are Lovely models, probably my favourite to paint of the new range. A real pleasure of detail, texture and interesting features. They speak to the more subtle and quietly terrifying facet of the Ogor race, the one that creeps up on you silently in a blizzard and you never know you were taken!!

Beastclaw Hunters and Sabrefangs.
Credit: @badusernametag

Ogor Mawtribes Hunters.
Credit: @badusernametag

These droogs follow my usual style for Ogors, red/grey/brown skin, drab colours all over, rusty weapons and armour with layers of texture. I’ve gone for a really dark (Atramant black, with Naples yellow highlight) colour for the draped skin cloak/gorgets and I’m planning to carry this through to a repaint on my Beastclaw monsters and then on into Glutthorns, Maulbeasts and the rest. Pale Ogors, dark and brooding beasts; hopefully it’s a nice contrast and brings a new element to a collection, without starting from scratch. Also in this instance, some dark colours adds to the air of stealth, is my idea…

Ogor Mawtribes Hunters.
Credit: @badusernametag

Ogor Mawtribes Hunters.
Credit: @badusernametag

Final Thoughts

Badusernametag: This range release has been really impressive for the whole Ogor Mawtribes army. No sub-faction has been neglected and some of the nicest models (IMHO) sit in the Beastclaw Raiders. You can now assemble an army of nice models in any of the sub-factions without compromising on the pedigree of your meat. The Battletome even facilities this with the Armies of Renown and these are not to shabby. There is no reason not to mix all of them together however and I am excited to get moar Thicc bodies on the table and make a messy dinner…

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Ogor Mawtribes Mawseekers
content:
Howdy hungry Goons! The Ogor Mawtribes have been starving for an update for years, now they swim in a delicious soup of new releases. Games Workshop were generous with a bounty of review models for us to chow down on! Read on to see what our team think of the delectable delicacies of the new Mawseekers sub-faction.

For the other Ogor meat on the menu, go here.

With this range refresh and new fluff for the Ogor Mawtribes a new sub-faction has emerged; The Mawseekers. The Butcher shamans and their howling Gorger packs have been bolstered by raving, fanatical Cleavers and grim, mystical Gutseers. Last but far from least at the feast the High Slaughtermaster, Redd the Maw has replaced the Slaughtermaster of old. 

The Ogor Mawtribes have finally had a fluff update and some story progression; this is long awaited and is driven by the new model line. The Mawseekers are a core part of this, a fanatical cult of GurgMagurg, the Gulping God. Expanded and refined, the Butchers are no longer simple shamans of the Gutbusters, they lead, "The Mawseekers, crazed fanatics in thrall to their race’s Gastro-Shamans and addicted to the spray of blood at Close quarters.” Brutal fare indeed...

What's New

  • Redd the Maw (Unique Hero, 160mm base)
  • Butcher (Hero, 50mm base)
  • 3 Cleavers/Gutseers (Multi-purpose kit, 40mm bases)
Mawseekers
Credit: Warhammer Community

Redd the Maw

Badusernametag: Redd the Maw is a gross and bombastic prophet of the Gulping God. Returned from a long wandering pilgrimage in Shyish, he preaches the purity of raw meat and the rise of the Ogor race. This model replaces the generic Slaughtermaster with a unique hero. This is kinda ironic, as the Slaughtermaster model was originally in fact a unique hero (Special Character) in the world that was. We spin in circles to the tune of the hungry realms…

Redd the Maw
Credit: Warhammer Community

Redd is one of two centrepiece models the banquet of Mawtribes have been graced with in this range refresh release, the other being Overtyrant Morga the Mighty. Whilst Morga is a massive smash monster hero, Redd follows the new tradition of slow Warmachine/Infantry centrepieces, featuring a gaggle of followers around them. Redd rides a massive chariot that bears his cauldron into battle, pulled by a slavering Gorger and flanked by two fanatical Gutseers. 

Redd is one of the biggest and meanest of Ogors. His cauldron, though reminiscent of the old Mawpot, is decorated with the new metal ‘coiled entrails’ design that features in the Mawseekers range on Gutseers Gutplates and the like. It’s a really nice visual motif. You also have the ‘toothed maw’ icon on the top of his ladle and at the front of the pot. This range has coined new iconography for the faction, as well as a solid and clearly recognisable design aesthetic. It’s a strong visual language and we’re eating it up!

I have mixed feelings about this kit; it's amazing to see new and developed sculpts for the Ogor Mawtribes and I love the new design direction, visual cues, and motifs. On the other hand, this model feels a little lazy in composition, and lacks the depth and interesting composition of other large centrepiece ensembles in the Age of Sigmar range.

More of that later; let's get it built!

Redd the Maw- Sprues

Redd the Maw- Sprues

This is quite a straightforward build: You put together the chariot/war-cauldron, add Red to the top, then add in the followers. The chariot is a little flimsy during assembly, however, and I would suggest a slightly different order of operations to build it.

  • Before starting the chassis as suggested, turn the page and assemble the cauldron.
  • Then go back and do the basic chassis.
  • Once you’ve got the first bit together (pic below) add the cauldron in, which locks it all together.
  • Then flip and do the wheels and hanging corpses.
  • Get the wheels on and LET THEM DRY.
  • Then come back and carry on.
Redd the Maw- basic chassis build
Credit: @badusernametag

Redd the Maw- Add the pot, to LOCK it all together.
Credit: @badusernametag

This assembly order allows the cauldron to lock the structure together and get it straight before you fiddle about with the details. Also, leaving the wheels to dry fully before moving on gives them the best strength and chance of being straight; too much movement whilst wet could bend them easily, as the connections are a little flimsy.

Redd the Maw- Upside down for wheels and corpse meat. Let it DRY
Credit: @badusernametag

Shout out to the amazing hanging corpses (cow-ish thing and human) the hang down behind the chariot. Very cool.

Best damn bits.
Credit: @badusernametag

Also a shout out to this absolute beast of a Gutseer weirdo, just casually offering forth a steaming handful of glistening entrails and looking out with the most menacing ever mien from under his Goth-Ogor hood.

Top goth Ogor!!
Redd the Maw
Credit: @badusernametag

Redd the Maw
Credit: @badusernametag

Having assembled this model I realise that whilst it has the same intention as other large models in AoS with hangers-on, it does not seem to have the considered composition of other comparable models. Unlike Kakakros (OBR), this is not a ‘scene’ that draws us in and tells a story; the characters are not connected and there isn’t a physical scenic element connecting them. I guess the nearest good companion would be Glutos Orscollion (Hedonites) on his Excess wagon. That model has many hangers-on, monstrous servants and characters that are all mounted onto the chariot and are clearly all connected in one scene. It’s also on an oval base, which the chariot, its many riders and the mutants pulling it fill nicely.

In this case, the scene doesn’t seem well composed; the Gutseers are just wandering alongside and I am left wondering why this couldn’t have just been on a small oval (the chariot itself would fit) and you could put it amongst your units. It’s also on a massive 160mm base and really seems a little lost on there. I think I would have like to have seen a chariot with more levels that brought the hangers-on into the scene more. Or perhaps some scenic elements that tied them all together. 

Over all this is a great model concept that I think could have had some more love put into it in terms of composition and delivery.

Redd the Maw
Credit: @badusernametag

For painting I went for fast and loose here, using only contrast paints, some washes and a bible highlight colour (pallid witch flesh) to get this to a tabletop standard quickly.

Everything was Zenthinel highlighted up to Wraithbone together on the base, then I took the goons (Gutseers) off to paint them separately.

The base I sprayed loosely with two Montana browns over the Wraithbone, for depth. I used a range of Contrast and washes, highlighting them all when wet only, this blending unifies the tone and makes for a better final cohesion. But is pretty fast and fun to do.

List of paints:

  • Pallid Witch Flesh
  • Nuln Oil
  • Agrax Earthshade
  • Ratling Grime
  • Black Templar
  • Apothecary White
  • Gilliuman Flesh
  • Militarum Green
  • Shyish Purple
  • Gore-Grunta Fur
  • Blood Angels Red

I don’t really do metallics anymore, but this would of course love some Warlock bronze and maybe some dirty verdigris over the top.

Redd the Maw
Credit: @badusernametag

Redd the Maw
Credit: @badusernametag

Butcher

Badusernametag: Okay stop the clock. This is it. The best and most saliva tingly gross Hero kit ever for AoS, and I’ll hang my apron on the statement. It’s dripping with character and for me, it sums up everything that is gruesome, brutal and delicious about this army! New Butcher
Credit: Warhammer Community

There are three new infantry heroes for the Mawtribes: The Tyrant, Grell Firefist and this Butcher. Whilst the Tyrant has a slew of amazing weapons, heads and adornments, this kit is just so characterful and charming I cannot help but love it more!

Butcher Sprues

You get two head options here, one bare and one hooded. Interestingly, I think the hooded one just crosses the line here from grotesquely dark to a bit-too-silly. It’s a fine balance, which this model otherwise captures so well! She is so pleased with herself and clearly so full of joy to be tearing that corpse apart, whilst happily swinging the cleaver for the next victim. It has an almost Nurgle-esque jolliness to it, that is rendered dark and terrifying by the gruesome corpse in her grip and the swinging cauldron full of blood and corpses at her waist. 

Ogor Mawtribes Butcher.
Credit: @badusernametag

The movement in the model, from the cauldron sloshing, to the rippling oozing flesh of her body is spot on. Gives a real dynamism to this monster of flesh and hungry menace. Her wild-eyed expression of feral joy speaks to her fanaticism and the folds of flesh and just right, best I’ve seen on any Ogor for how the fluff and art speak for the army. This model is bigger than the other heroes and dominates its 50mm base. This will really stand out amongst the other Mawseekers.

It’s a clever kit to assemble, but unlike some others, the pieces slot together just so and this is a really fast build. Not a niggle or complaint. When I first saw this I really wanted to convert it into my mounted Overtyrant (Bolga Braindrinker), but now I must buy another, as it is just too damn cool not to paint up and join the Mawseekers throng!

Ogor Mawtribes Butcher.
Credit: @badusernametag

Cleavers/Gutseers

Cleavers on the block
Credit: @badusernametag

Norman: These went together relatively easily, but there was a good amount of bit hunting that I needed to do to find the pieces I needed. The poses themselves are great, they're very open and are pretty simple to customize with the rest of the range if that's something you're looking to do. Aesthetically, they do a great job of repeating design language from the Butcher and Redd, which helps differentiate them from their non-Mawseeker friends.

Badusernametag: Much as I love the new Butcher, this really is the infantry kit for me. Of the new infantry kits, this is the only one to feature multiple build options (more than one unit) and I quite love that the differences are subtle, as it allows for a bit of wiggle and customisation in your build. You could build this kit 3-4 times and have some mixed and interesting units to show for it.

Cleaver Champion and Gutseer Champion- new BFFs!!!
Redd the Maw
Credit: @badusernametag

Broadly, the Cleavers are like mini-Butchers, with ragged apron gut plates and two chopping weapons apiece (a mix of cleavers, knives, hooks) and the champion carries a swinging cauldron of gore, much like their Butcher masters. The Gutseers have hoods, one weapon and a gristly totem in the other hand made from an icon and part of a corpse. The Gutseers also have the ‘coiled entrails’ metalwork motif on their gut plate, which is super cool.

Cleaver Champion
Credit: @badusernametag

Interesting that the two unit champions are made from different base models, which means that you can build both out of one kit. Why would you? Not sure! But I did, as I wanted to see what the thickest and meanest of the Mawseekers had to offer. Both the builds have real appeal and I’m sure that we will see many of both on the tabletop. I have used the ‘coiled entrails’ gut plates on all my models here though, as its a really great motif I just can’t resist! 

Can’t wait to get the rest of them painted and on the table.

Ogor Mawtribes Cleaver.
Credit: @badusernametag

Norman:

Gutseer Credit: MildNorman

These paint up pretty fast! not too many doodads on them nor too much complexity to them. The new skin textures on these guys do a lot to helping washes push your shadows a bit more and adds some visual interest to the huge swathes of skin. The materials are easily differentiated and the poses are wide open which makes painting a breeze. This one guy took me about 3 hours primer to done not counting drying times for washes and basing but a lot of that time was spent figuring out a scheme. If you're going in with a plan, I expect folks can bang out a reinforced unit of these in a couple of painting sessions.

Final Thoughts

Badusernametag: This is a great release for those into the meaty and bloody end of things in the Ogor Mawtribes army. With these new kits and the gorgeous Gorgers (which are only a couple of years old) you can make the core of a gruesome army with all new models and a strong new theme. Throw in some Gluttons and a Tyrant and it’s going to look great and smash hard. 

All these new kits fit together so well, go together easily and are a joy to paint. This is a release I had such high hopes for and it really has not disappointed me.

title: Tabletop Battles App Updates for August, 2026: StarCraft, Age of Sigmar, and More
content:
We've been working long hours to update the Tabletop Battles App for game tracking purposes and we're happy to announce that we've got another great round of updates today. Last Time Around we talked about adding maps, terrain measurements, and Faction trackers to the app, so if you've been looking for a way to track things like Combat Doctrines, Blessings of Khorne, Pain Tokens, or Contagions, we've got you covered.

If you haven't downloaded the app yet, you can get it through one of the links below:

Today's update is live on Android and will be available in the next few days on iOS. This week we have some big update news we're happy to share.

Support for the StarCraft Miniatures game

The Tabletop Battles App now supports StarCraft: The Miniatures Game! In addition to just tracking your score, you can track things like: active supply, current supply cap, and drafted missions/deployments. Every mission is also implemented in the app, giving you guided scoring for all of your objectives.

Loading...

Looking forward, we’ll be looking at more ways to improve the app beyond just supporting new releases. We’re looking into tracking your Vespene Gas cards so you don’t have to have your cards with you at all times as well as other quality of life features that’ll improve your games at home. As always, the app is 100% free and you can get started tracking your StarCraft Games as early as right now (app store weirdness notwithstanding).

Loading...

We worked directly with Archon on this one and we're happy to show off the slickest interface we've built yet for tracking games.

Warhammer Age of Sigmar: 2026 General's Handbook

It's long overdue, but we've also added support for the 2026 General's Handbook from Age of Sigmar. So if you've been waiting for that one, we've got you covered with all of the new missions. We're still working on the deployment maps/battleplans for that one, so bear with us as we get them implemented.

Warhammer 40,000: Quality of Life Updates

We've been continuing to tweak and improve the player experience for Warhammer 40k, responding to bug fixes and requests. Some of this update's changes:

  • Fixed the bug which sent you back to the player screen when picking a mission
  • Pulled out the two missions that hid some scoring behind a button
  • Added descriptions to some faction trackers to make it clearer what's being selected
  • Fixed some bugs around mission scoring
  • Added scoring descriptions to some missions to clarify when scoring happens

What's Next?

We're working on a few more Quality of life improvements (such as auto-selecting the recommended primary mission for your disposition in 40k), including adding integration with Best Coast Pairings. Soon you'll be able to connect events and submit games directly for StarCraft, Age of Sigmar, and Kill Team. We're also adding Exodites for Kill Team next week.

Why Use Our App?

We've seen this question pop up once or twice from players who aren't familiar with our app, or whose introduction is the War Journal in the Warhammer 40,000 app. Well, there are a few reasons:

  • Runs faster and better. Tabletop Battles is built in Flutter and not React. Flutter is less common but removes a lot of runtime jank that can bog down React Native apps. If you've noticed that TTBA runs faster, this is a primary reason why. Flutter generally outperforms React Native and uses less CPU and as a result, less battery.
  • Built-in stats screens. If you want more than just a list of your games, we've got you covered, and we're working on more personal stats you can access via our Edge web app.
  • Faction trackers. If you want to track things like Pain tokens or Saga progress, our app has that.
  • Other game modes. Do you want to play asymmetric missions? track custom games? Do you need a different disposition than the one you're allowed to select? The Tabletop Battles interface is much more flexible, and allows for custom score input.
  • Direct feedback. We read every bug report and work to implement changes, and we respond to inquiries on Discord. The Tabletop Battles app is very much what you help make it.

Also it's free - we don't get any money from you using our app. If anything, it costs us money. We're just in it to make the best possible app for tracking games of tabletop wargames.

So if you haven't already, give the app a download and check out our newest features. They're available today on Android and likely this weekend for iOS.

title: Century of the Vampire: The Tier List
content:
The List

Thank you to this specific Tiermaker template for providing the base for this image; I added a couple things in myself. It's not on them that they didn't have a 40K animated series from 2021. They did have The Batman vs. Dracula!

Here is our master page for Century of the Vampire, with links to reviews for every movie pictured above. Below, I'll shout some out specifically and explain some of my decision-making.

The Words

Sixty-two films over a year and a half or so; hardly an exhaustive look at all vampire cinema -- you can find lists of more than English-language 200 films without even looking too hard, to say nothing of the films from various European and Asian cinemas we lightly touched on at best -- but I think we got the big ones in terms of cultural impact; the high notes and the low notes. I’ve sorted the films into tiers, as is the modern custom, from S to F. I anticipated a bell curve that saw very few S and F films and the majority of the offerings ending up in B and C; that’s almost what happened -- if you combine B and C together into a vast undifferentiated middle, then that blob does in fact outnumber the As or the Ds by itself. The way I thought about that ranking was that B films were mediocre in a positive fashion -- fun-bad or fun or almost-good -- and C films were, well, just mediocre. As I discuss the tiers I’ll talk about the film I had at the top of each tier, the film I had at the bottom, and the film in the tier whose placement there surprised me the most; we won’t go through all 16 films in the D tier, for instance, in a specific order of quality. At a certain point of granularity it just becomes completely arbitrary, and frankly I’m not willing to think about nonsense like “which Twilight movie is better than the rest of the Twilight movies” ever again.

S-Tier

Here we have three films that I think epitomize the best instincts of modern Western vampire cinema, each in a very different way. Blade remains the high water mark of vampires as action/science fiction blockbuster monsters; I’d say “often imitated, never duplicated” but no one actually seems interested in making a movie like this anymore, certainly not Marvel themselves, who remain paralyzed by their inability to shove Blade into their nice, neat Cinematic Universe typology. Shadow of the Vampire is almost certainly the scariest of the vampire films I watched for this feature; the looming horror, the creeping dread, the growing realization that while the Schreck creature is indeed a monster, he is not the only one haunting these proceedings and might not even be the worst of them. Vampire movies struggle to actually be scary in the visceral ways that gore-soaked and jump-scare addicted slashers and the like manage, so they have to make up for it in spades with both intellectual and vibes-based horror. Shadow of the Vampire is the best of the bunch at that. And Only Lovers Left Alive is at the complete other end of the spectrum; it is the best example in the dataset of vampires as social, sexy creatures -- they hunt and kill in the film, yes, but it is not a horror movie. It’s just as much hangout cinema as anything else Jim Jarmusch has ever made, and as a director he is very much a sometimes food for me. Here, it hits. This is the one category where I don’t have a best or worst; I think I prefer Blade the least of the three as I enter middle age, but it would top this list 20 years ago. Only Lovers Left Alive is the clear surprise here; I had very low expectations going in, though part of that was his terrible zombie movie (made years later) leaving a bad taste in my mouth. In every way, zombies are the inferior movie monster.

A-Tier

An expected list of vampire mainstays; the recently-released Sinners is on here, along with Coppola's Dracula, del Toro’s Cronos, Park’s Thirst, Schumacher’s The Lost Boys, both version of the Let Me/the Right One In, Jordan’s Interview with the Vampire, every version of Nosferatu we looked at, and…Dracula Untold? Yes, this is the movie that defines the bottom of our A-Tier; it’s surprising to you that it’s here, probably, but not to me. This is the closest we’ve come to a great vampire action flick since the original Blade, and it’s very unfortunate that it got caught up in the Dark Universe nonsense because I think Luke Evans does a great job in it. Unironic fan of the Bat Punch and Bat Slam. I think Near Dark is the best of the bunch here; I think Shadow of the Vampire was the best horror vampire film in the bunch but Near Dark is easily the meanest. It would probably be in the S-Tier if I was being slightly less restrictive on that grade. The most surprising entry here to me is the video game Vampire: The Masquerade Bloodlines 2, which I thought would be a disaster. It was instead merely a flop, but I still found the story, linear as it is, extremely compelling. Great vampire stuff.

B-Tier

We’ve got El Conde at the top, a bit too long and inconsistent to get into the A-Tier but with great individual images and moments, which is sort of the epitome of the kind of film that ends up in the B-Tier. From Dusk Till Dawn would likewise be up a tier if the first thirty minutes weren’t intolerable; the version of that film you have in your head from when you watched it when you were 13, where it starts out with them arriving at the bar, that’s an A-Tier bordering on S-Tier film. Its placement here is probably the tier’s biggest surprise. 30 Days of Night is a rock-solid B-Tier film by our rubric; it’s also a pretty mean film, but it’s dragged down in places by how aggressively 2010s it is. Every time I look at the original Underworld on the end of the list here I’m tempted to go back and bump it down to the top of the C-Tier. It was certainly a much more successful movie than Blade II, and it certainly has fewer weird bumps and rough edges than that movie does, but that’s about the best that can be said for it -- and is part of the overall argument that the B and C-Tiers are really expressions of the same general silo of films.

C-Tier

Blade II makes it into the B-Tier when I’m specifically thinking of the monster design on the freakish bug vampire Nosferatu creatures; then I think of literally anything else about the movie and it’s back to the C-Tier. But that’s good enough for the top of the tier! The movie I’m most surprised is down here is the original Dracula; that’s a very poor adaptation with way too much time spent on the Renfield character, and notable basically only for Lugosi himself. The ratio of interesting shots to boring flab in Nadja sadly puts it down here instead of higher up, though that is a film whose Renfield I very much enjoy. Three of the four Underworld sequels live at the bottom of this group, with Evolution mainly still up here to form a firm floor to differentiate from…

D-Tier

Cirque du Freak: The Vampire’s Assistant gets place of privilege here just because John C. Reilly is working his ass off to get leading man bookings. It doesn’t work, but he really does try. Bad film, though. The animated feature The Batman vs. Dracula is down here because I didn’t have anywhere else to put it; it’s a Batman cartoon where he fights Dracula. It won’t surprise you. John Carpenter’s Vampires? Check. Dracula 2000? Check. Vampire in Brooklyn? Check. The Nineties were great for vampires but they also churned out some real dreck (Dracula 2000 came out before 9/11, so it counts as part of the Nineties). All the Twilights are down here so I don’t have to think about them. To give you an idea of how far down D-Tier can stretch without getting to F-Tier, Morbius is down here too. The CGI vampire fighting stuff is cool enough to give it some redeeming value; I think that’s actually the surprise here, that it’s this high on the list. Ultraviolet forms the floor for the D-Tier, in a very similar place to Near Dark but in absolute inversion: If I wasn’t keeping the F-Tier exclusive, it’d be down there.

F-Tier

For a very, very long time there was only one film in this tier: BloodRayne. I kept this entire tier cleared out for this unprofessional, intractable piece of garbage, too lazy and boring to be repulsive; in this respect it is unlike the man who directed it, who manages all three with ease. There’s little I can say about it that I haven’t already said, except that in the time since I wrote my review he returned to “prominence” with a work that’s more an act of criminal incitement than a film, Citizen Vigilante. Simply one of the most contemptible to have ever done it, holistically.

Then Vampire Academy came along. I wrote in the Vampire Academy review that the film didn’t “threaten [BloodRayne’s position] directly” as a matter of craft, and I do believe that; it is at the very low bounds of professionalism, perhaps, but it was a professionally-made movie. But whereas a good director and writer can probably do something acceptable with BloodRayne -- it’s never making S-Tier and probably not A-Tier, but you can certainly see the possibilities of a B-Tier film there -- Vampire Academy is just unacceptable in its bones. It’s a soulless attempt to cash in on Harry Potter while doing a significant amount of race science along the way, disastrously conceived from the jump to be nothing but easy money from undiscerning young readers and viewers. Though the physical production and actor work is up to standard (mostly; the male lead is badly stumbling through his lines trying to act in a language he clearly doesn’t speak), the scriptwriting and plotting might actually be more incompetent than BloodRayne. In the end, the thing that distinguishes it from BloodRayne at the bottom of this list is its contempt for the concept of vampirism; “vampire” is just a brand to slap on an extremely shitty and boring private school YA story that has a little bit of poorly-thought out magic attached to it. It had the temerity to end on a sequel hook that, thank Christ, it never got. They tried it again as a Peacock show and while I’m sure they took more liberties with the material that time to make it less putrid, a bad foundation never leads to a good house. At least we’ll always have the CHVRCHES cover of Bela Lugosi’s Dead.

Final Thoughts

And that’s the wrap on the project! This leg of it, at least. Vampires aren’t just movie monsters these days. They make video games about them too. I covered one in this series because it had just come out and I needed to break up the string of Twilight films, but we’ll probably be doing a more thorough examination of their contributions to that form of media somewhere down the line.

title: Can Warhammer 40k's 11th edition starter set teach me the glory of the Emperor?
content:
Warhammer 40k's 11th edition has arrived with a healthy crop of boxes to entice new players (or those just wanting a good deal on a big bunch of minis). One of these, the 11th edition starter set, is specifically intended to teach you the game, with all the dice, rulers, minis, and terrain you need, plus a booklet designed to walk you through the experience.

Apparently 40k has a reputation for slightly shaky starter sets, and while I own a surprising amount of Warhammer and have painted a fair few minis, setting them up on my table and rolling some dice is a Rubicon I have yet to cross. Until now that is. What better way to test the starter set than to give it to someone who is actually just starting?

Will I be brought around to worship the Emperor and his glorious dice? Or will I slink off somewhere to… I don't know, join Nurgle or something. This metaphor got away from me, but cut me some slack, we're in a multi-month heatwave here.

What's inside?

When it comes to the contents, the 11th edition 40k starter set is sort of like the Armageddon-lite. On the Ork side it has a Warboss, 20 Boyz (two of them Nobs), 10 Gretchin, a Wartrakk, and the wonderful new Weirdboy. Compared to Armageddon you're missing out on a Big Mek, Bannernob, Painboy, and Bigboss. If you're purely counting model numbers, that doesn't seem like much!

Since it's a more elite army, the Space Marine side has less than half the models total. Here we have a Captain, Librarian, 5 Intercessors, 5 Vanguard Veterans, and the new Land Speeder. Compared to Armageddon, we're lacking 5 Intercessors, 3 Eradicators, a Chaplain, and an Ancient standard bearer.

Obviously, you save a lot compared to what you'd pay buying all these models separately, though the value proposition gets shakier if you're not interested in all of these models. If you're brand new, it seems like the best option would be to go halvsies and split the box's contents with a mate, rather than starting two armies at the same time.

There's also six sprues of pretty terrain!

Building

Constructing these minis was an enjoyable experience as ever, though I found I disagreed with the order of operations on some of the more densely detailed Space Marine characters. I'm a little wary of push-fit models, usually preferring to cut the pegs off and glue the minis together for a snugger fit. I tried to do it 'authentically' here though for the sake of the review. For the Imperium half of the box, this worked out fine, the bulky armor disguising any imperfect joins. The Xenos side was another story though, with some particularly irksome gaps standing out right in the middle of the Orks shoulder pads. I quickly caved and went back to my old ways for the remainder of my minis.

While I'm still in the early stages of painting these creations, one thing I should note is that this box is lacking a transfer sheet. I gaslit myself into thinking I'd misplaced one, but nope - it's just not included. Which is a little annoying!

Learning

The 'learn to play' section talks you through four scenarios, gradually explaining the rules and introducing new models and complexity. At first, you just have two characters hacking away at each other in melee. Then moving and charging is covered, followed by the shooting phase. And finally, you learn how to actually score points with a strategic objective.

This all works very nicely as a stepwise way to learn the basics. It explains some rules to you, presents a scenario, then talks you through each step of that scenario, reminding you what you just learned. Perfect.

I do have a few minor gripes, though. For instance, the book contains tables reminding you how to calculate wound and save rolls, and it would be great to have a handout for these. They're included again in a quick reference section near the back (and by scenario 4 I'd almost got it memorized), but this might've worked better as a separate sheet to avoid unnecessary rulebook flicking.

The set up section could also be made more visually clear as well. For instance, it was not obvious to me where terrain was supposed to be placed and what kind of terrain I should be using. The unit list also drew no distinction between a nob and a regular ork boy, forcing me to squint at an unclear top-down image to work out if the former should be in each scenario or not. These seem like small issues, but it left me feeling uncertain, and worried that I wasn't doing it 'right'.

However, my primary issue with this learning section is that I wish it was a little longer. It ends with strategic objectives, then contains just one page discussing the command phase and stratagems. I would've loved to have another scenario or even two playing around with these, with the book demonstrating how different tactics can help you win a match.

It feels like I was just approaching the point where Warhammer becomes an actual game instead of a die-rolling combat simulator, but hadn't quite got there yet.

In fact, while this set does a good job of teaching the mechanics very straightforwardly, it doesn't ever go into detail about how you might play the game in different ways in order to actually try and win. It's a competent rules-teacher, but not a great game-teacher, if that makes any sense.

Overall, I feel like the starter set is a decent jumping off point, but I'm left feeling like the best way to learn Warhammer is probably to have someone else who already knows the ancient art inside out show you the ropes.

title: Why Critical Role's Sallowlands series didn't grip me as much as I'd hoped
content:
That's a wrap for Critical Role's second Age of Umbra mini-series. There were many heartening moments in such a miserable setting, thanks to some stellar performances from the cast. Sallowlands, however, never gripped me the way a mainline series does. In fact, now it's over, my first thought was 'I can't wait for campaign four to come back'.

I've thought long and hard about why things haven't hit me the way I'd hoped, and I've boiled it down to a few key factors:

The system

I don't think Daggerheart is a bad tabletop RPG (if you've read my recent Hope and Fear review, you'll know I'm actually quite the fan). I do think it's an unfamiliar one for most of the Sallowlands cast.

D&D, for all its flaws, is like a comfy pair of slippers for most roleplayers. We know its cadence so well that we barely need to think about how a scene (or our DnD classes) works. That familiarity is crucial for a show like Critical Role, where I'm mostly watching to become invested in the story, not the system itself.

I don't enjoy watching Laura Bailey, brilliant battle strategist that she is, because I want to see how her character tackles combat with a vampire. I want to see her bring a character to life (and maybe death) in an emotional, nuanced, and exciting way.

D&D is the vehicle for the stories that Critical Role usually tells. The character arcs come to the forefront, and the rules fade into the background.

That doesn't happen so much in Sallowlands. I think it's because the cast are still getting to grips with Daggerheart as an actual play system. Bailey and her fellow Critical Role co-founder Matt Mercer will be more familiar than most - but even they've had just a few years of Daggerheart versus a few decades of D&D.

The rest of the cast are even more alien to it. In fact, with varied backgrounds and experience levels, almost all of them are making their Critical Role debut. That's even more waters to test before dipping your toe in.

A lack of experience isn't a problem, but it creates an atmosphere that feels markedly different. It's less performance and more play.

'Above table' discussion, as the Critical Role team call it, wades into the fray more often, breaking immersion. At times, a player's immediate focus on how the game actually works means they have less to give to spontaneous character moments. Those moments often make an entire episode. We do still get them in Sallowlands (I've never recovered from the 'Mr Beaks' escapade), but they're further and fewer between.

I want to stress that the performances in Age of Umbra are fantastic. I sincerely hope Jennifer English and Abubakar Salim appear in more actual play shows, because they were the standout stars of Sallowlands. They brought real heart to the party, with both silly and severe moments carried wonderfully.

Vico Ortiz, too, shines as Caguama. If English and Salim are a top-notch double-act, Ortiz is an eloquent solo artist. They're almost always found at center stage in Sallowlands' most emotional moments. Without Caguama, the story's pace and punch would have suffered greatly.

Talking of pace…

The structure

We get far less time with these characters than we would in a typical campaign. Again, this isn't a problem in isolation - there are many fantastic mini-series in the world. But, in the case of Sallowlands, Critical Role's storytelling struggles with this limitation.

With less time to tease backstories, there's less emotional impact when characters reveal something personal. I'm nowhere near as upset when they die (and, because this is Age of Umbra, several of them do).

What's worse, the cast seem in a hurry to create the kind of arcs we'd expect from months of standard campaign play. There's a rush to ascribe more meaning to the events of Sallowlands than the series has actually earned.

At one time, English's character describes the rest of the party as 'found family'. Given how little time they've practically spent together (and how few of the scenes show them doing anything other than fighting or exploring), this feels insincere.

Perhaps this is a flaw in the setup more than anything else. English, Salim, and Bailey all play characters with pre-existing relationships, but for the most part, this party of five is thrown together entirely by circumstance. Everyone heard rumors of a city that could save them, and they're sticking together because it makes sense for survival.

This sets up player goals that are simple and external. It gives us a structure of play that feels passive, like the world is happening to our cast rather than being impacted by them. That's a far cry from the living, breathing city streets of Aramán.

Speaking of setting…

The setting

The Halcyon Domain, Mercer's setting for Age of Umbra, is a dreary, depressing place. We visit dank swamps and cages, dust-filled wastelands, and towers of desperate zealots. It's very Bloodborne, and in a world where Soulslikes are dime a dozen, I feel like I've seen it all before.

None of the scenery stands out in Sallowlands. That's a real shame when so much of Daggerheart's system gamifies the environments you traverse. Exploration is more important here than in a game like D&D, and less attention to detail has been given by our narrator.

Almost none of the NPCs stick in your mind, either. Mercer isn't giving his best performances as Bowen, the straggler the party picks up on their journey. And beyond him, I can only recall one a handful of other notable figures - the charming cajun merchant who bought Mr Beaks from Caguama, and the delightfully disgusting boss we face in the finale.

Mercer's guidance (or lack of it) lets the series down more than anything else, I think. He is single-handedly responsible for creating the show's backdrop. When that background is bland, the rest of the details can all-too-easily start to blur together. Things become harder to follow (and, when episodes are several hours long, you really need to give your audience reasons to pay attention).

There's a point in Sallowlands where Zachery Renauldo says "we've come too far to not know what's going on". It wasn't meant to, but it summed up a lot of my feelings about Sallowlands. There are some utterly wonderful singular moments, but the sum of its parts were passive and, at worst, forgettable. It didn't quite work, however much I wanted it to.

Want to share your own thoughts on Age of Umbra: Sallowlands? I'm always keen to chat about actual play in the Wargamer Discord.
