title: BattleTech Fiction Focus: These Violent Ends by Bryan Young
content:
Well, here we are, folks! Over the course of the year so far, we've seen the publication of Bryan Young's first three novellas telling stories from the Dominion Civil War (along with an interview I did with the author about the first book), and today, August 14th, the final(-ish) volume of the series drops! Say hello to These Violent Ends!

We'd like to thank Bryan for providing us with an advance copy of These Violent Ends for our review!

Image Credit: Catalyst Game Labs

Oh, what's that? That (-ish) up there? Well, I'm pleased to share with y'all that a collected edition of the series should be out around the end of 2026 or the beginning of ‘27, and it will include a bonus novella, Defy The Stars, which will advance the Dominion's timeline into… drumroll please… 3153! That's right, we're making it into a whole new in-universe calendar year with the next one!

That said, Strider and Vesper's main arc does reach a culmination here in These Violent Ends, and the tetralogy on its own does feel like a complete story… mostly.

Let's dive in and take a closer look, shall we?

It's somewhat difficult to discuss an ending in earnest without discussing its, well, ending, so while I'm not going to go into full details here, there will be some spoilers in this review, to a somewhat greater degree than most of my reviews. You have been warned.

Clan Ghost Bear Locust IIC. Credit: Jack Hunter

After the end of the last novella saw Vesper reassigned to the Third Freemen and, specifically, to her ex Strider's Star as a vindictive punishment for her Denier views, this chapter in their story quickly jumps forward to the Third's next invasion target: The over-bright, highly-toxic, fungus-ridden planet of Tarazed, defended by the newly-mercenary-again Fifth McCarron's Armored Cavalry.

There's plenty to like here (in fact, I found These Violent Ends engaging enough to finish in a single sitting!), but I'm sorry to say that this might be the weakest installment of the Dominion Civil War Tetralogy. The creative structure of the earlier novellas is basically gone: The only in-universe document (and only continuation of the story on Grumium, so central to the first two novellas!) in These Violent Ends is a single letter from Strider's father, and the novella is bookended by BattleTech-conventional looks into the halls of power on Luthien (and, at the end, Rasalhague). Those scenes are handled well enough (Prince Miraborg's cocky turn in the spotlight, in particular, is as memorable as it is brief), but the flavor of the earlier books’ biased reporting is lost… and isn't even replaced by less biased in-universe reporting, somewhat undermining this book's stated theme of the triumph of truth over factionalism.

The military SF aspect of the book's plot is pretty uncomplicated. The tactical situation on the planet allows the Big MAC force to largely play keepaway, frustrating Star Colonel Rand's desire for a decisive battle, and the inhospitable nature of Tarazed's surface, which we're told forces most human habitats underground, is used to keep civilians out of the book entirely. We're told that the Bears land and set up their HQ in an empty city, with absolutely no explanation for why or how it's empty, and while the 5th McCarron's encampment is ostensibly atop a population center, we never see or hear anything of the locals. There was barely any more from the people of Yamarovka in By Civil Blood Betrayed, but at least we were given something there. Both these last two outings, while relatively starved for page count, stand in sharp contrast to the focus this very series gave to the people of Grumium in its first two installments, to say nothing of the native population's importance to Young's Ghosts of Timkovichi. This feels like a step backwards onto safer, more familiar ground.

Tarazed is functionally just a backdrop, though, for the gradual easing of tensions between Strider and Vesper. This has echoes of Dexter and Rhiannon's arc in Young's Outfoxed, but in a positive change, we see much more from Vesper here than we did from Rhi there, and this relationship arc plays out with pretty good pacing.

This is your second spoiler warning, this is approximately the point where I go further than my typical book reviews.

McCarron's Armored Cavalry Assault Lance. Credit: Jack Hunter

The Shakespearean ambitions of the Dominion Civil War tetralogy’s titles are somewhat undone, however, by a relatively comfortable ending. The tragedy and loss of These Violent Ends’ violent end happen all around Strider and Vesper, but leave the central couple relatively unscathed, reunited, and able to redirect all their dissatisfaction with Rasalhagian politics towards uncomplicated bad actors like Star Colonel Rand.

I've gradually come to feel that villains are probably the weakest part of Bryan Young's writing… while they're often memorable, they usually have next-to-no nuance. Star Colonel Rand here and in A Question of Survival, Colonel Hachtel-Steiner in Ghosts of Timkovichi, Leon Hansen in Outfoxed, Nikita Malthus in Without Question… all of them are myopically violent, thoroughly convinced of their own justness (bar a couple moments of near-miss self-reflection from Leon), and thoroughly despicable. One could argue that's true to the reality we see out our windows these days, but the BattleTech universe is one beautifully gifted with room for nuance. We do see some noble antagonists in Young's fiction, like Emilio Hall in A Question of Survival and MechWarrior Coote in Ghosts of Timkovichi, and a few just-here-to-do-a-job antagonists (Colonel Jason Anthony of These Violent Ends’ Fifth McCarron's is a simple career soldier who was just the only person willing to take command of the Fifth after Daoshen Liao executed their previous commander, for instance), but these are usually overshadowed by a more directly villainous figure.

While Strider and Vesper reach an agreement that Rand is emblematic of the rot at the heart of the Dominion by the end of this book, she does not see her comeuppance in These Violent Ends. Likewise, the Dominion's invasion of Tarazed, and of the Combine as a whole, grinds down to a stalemate, and Grumium's internal conflicts are seemingly neatly resolved offscreen, along with the biggest drivers of internal strife in the Dominion. To a degree, a lack of plot closure is simply the nature of shared-universe fiction in an ongoing setting - every story ends on The Adventure Continues - but for the BattleTech metaplot, we're at an odd place in the ilClan story.

Catalyst has signaled a desire to move on from the sourcebook-driven metaplot advancement we saw across Shattered Fortress > ilClan > Tamar Rising > Dominions Divided > Empire Alone > ilKhan's Eyes Only, in favor of a fiction-first approach, but it has also seemed fairly cautious and conservative with how far its novels advance the ongoing story, with most ilClan fiction only providing little crumbs and nibbles of forward movement, typically stopping short of any major fallout or consequences of each book's events.

On the whole, I've counseled those frustrated by The Long 3152 to keep patience: There are, after all, plenty of plot hooks to explore in the immediate wake of the ilClan Trial, and BattleTech is hardly in 40k-tier stasis as a larger setting, but I'd say it's the Dominion Civil War tetralogy's move on from Grumium, specifically, that bugs me. That planet and its people seemed so close to the heart of this series throughout its first two volumes, but it simply becomes an afterthought as soon as Strider and Vesper move offworld to join the war effort against the Combine. Maybe Defy The Stars will bring the focus back to the home front, and/or maybe Star Colonel Rand will finally suffer the karmic backlash she richly deserves by this point, but as it stands, These Violent Ends peculiarly feels both like it is an end to this story and like it isn't.

Kodiak. Credit: porble

Looking back over the Dominion Civil War series as a (near) whole, it feels oddly disjointed for a serial story with tight continuity and a single author. The structure varies, from the strictly limited-PoV which so enchanted me in Star-Crossed Warriors to the conventional BattleTech flow of These Violent Ends, while plot focus wavers between larger issues, like Grumium's political situation in the first two books, and tight personal focus, with These Violent Ends only rarely straying beyond the tiny bubble of Strider and Vesper's Star. Star-Crossed, I felt, managed its split focus very ably and organically, but that compelling structure broke down over the course of the series, and here at the end… this is a good, solid, enjoyable BattleTech story, but it's not all that groundbreaking, not all that profound. Had its first book not set the bar so high, in my estimation, I might not be disappointed with that, but as it stands, it feels like this was a series which had the potential to be truly great, but ended up merely good.

That said, “merely good” is still good, and I think this book, and this whole series, is well worth checking out if Strider and Vesper's character arc has engaged you at all, and it's still got some good things to offer any fan of the involved factions, even if you, like a poster I was speaking with the other day in TTB's Discord server, are turned off by the “YA Romance” nature of its central couple's beginnings.

When I next see you, BattleTech fiction fans, I plan to broaden the scope of my articles to give new and returning players a, “Where are we and how did we get here?” primer to the ilClan era of the Inner Sphere, as highlighted in Catalyst's new Core product line. Talk to you then!

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: For the Emperor (Illustrated and Annotated Edition), by Sandy Mitchell
content:
Image credit: Games Workshop

Sometimes things are best enjoyed in small doses. We all like cake, for instance, but not a lot of us would put their hand up for the opportunity to sit down and eat a whole one in one sitting. Today's book, For the Emperor, is just such a treat- but in order to best explain why we need to start on the other side of the equation here, the side that eats the whole cake.

For the Emperor originally released in 2003, following Ciaphas Cain's introduction in a couple of short stores published in the pages of Inferno! Magazine (Fight or Flight and The Beguiling). The self-interested Imperial Commissar and malodorous aide Jurgen's brand of dark comedy in a grimdark universe was a significant stylistic reach for Black Library audiences of the time, but it proved a roll of the dice that paid off.

Ultimately, author Sandy Mitchell would pen nearly a dozen novels in the series, culminating with 2024's Vainglorious after a six-year series pause. He very quickly figured out what elements resonated with readers and relentlessly delivered. When Cain's sophomore novel Caves of Ice entered the Black Library Readers' Hall of Fame, Committee member Michael Dodd of Track of Words noted:

This is really where it becomes clear that the Cain series is going to become the AC/DC of Black Library. That the whole point of the series is to hit the same beats and play the same jokes, because those beats and those jokes are just so damn good! There’s nothing wrong with wanting more of the same.

There's certainly something to say for giving the people what they want. And yet...

Meanwhile, on Gravalax

Cain's kickoff novel sees him assigned to a Valhallan split regiment, one comprised of the remnants of two different understrength ones. Cain must find a way to get both halves of his new deployment to work in unity with one another, all the while as they're stationed on a world riven by tensions between the Imperium and the tau, which have a strong trade and diplomatic presence on the planet.

That fragile detente is repeatedly threatened by attack and assassination, the pro-Imperial citizens clashing with the pro-tau separatists. Alongside Inquisitor Amberley Vail, Cain must find out what's behind all the trouble before conflict with the tau slips into a shooting war.

All the while, Cain continually seeks to preserve his own skin, continually managing to fail upwards through a combination of sheer dumb luck, keen survival instinct, and timely assistance from those around him.

Image credit: Games Workshop

Cain Fatigue

The past year has seen me increasingly enjoying Black Library's range of audiobooks. With so much of my paper reading in service to Tabletop Battles reviewing the latest releases, audio has been a fun way for me to catch up on the backlog of older books and revisit some of the classics (you can find those reviews here). But as I've worked in Mitchell's Cain catalogue, the less I've come away enjoying it. Heresy, right?

It's not that the books are bad, far from it! There's good reason that Mitchell's seen four of them end up immortalized in the Hall. They're both very popular, and were a great early example of what could happen when you were allowed to push the boundaries of the setting in directions they'd not really been before.

It's just that as Mitchell has returned to the same wellspring of inspiration, it becomes increasingly clear when read in quick succession just how repetitive they can get. In my review of Steve Lyons' The Relentless Dead I discussed the idea of "Flanderization," indicating "the gradual reduction of a character into its most oversimplified and exaggerated traits." The term was coined by TVTropes, describing the process by which Ned Flanders became more and more a caricature of himself over successive seasons of The Simpsons.

Yes, Mitchell hits the same beats, AC/DC style, across the series, but at the same time the series noticeably starts to Flanderize. The occasional mention of Jurgen's more piquant qualities, for instance, quickly loses its humor when the man can't even be in a scene without a joke at his expense. For this reason, I typically recommend enjoying Cain more as an occasional palate-cleanser than an all-in bingeworthy experience.

Or put another way- since the more you eat the less you enjoy each bite- I suggest it's best devoured as an occasional slice of cake.

Image credit: Games Workshop

Impressions

I bring all of this up to set the table for what was the most surprising realization for me as I read For the Emperor again (this time, of course, with the annotations): this book is so damn good. 

That probably sounds obvious, but as someone who has soured a bit on the repetitiveness of the series it was delightful to see it how clean a tale Mitchell wrote when he wasn't leaning in to the things that made the book popular after publication. 75% of the Jurgen body odor jokes...gone. Just a few sprinklings of the "if I'd known then what I know now, I would have [not done the thing I'm about to do]" constructions, a reasonable amount of his internal cowardice monologuing... all of those "Cain doing Cain things" or "Cain being Cain" moments in balance with the traditional narrative elements of the book instead of shading them out... if there had to be a formula, this was the one to use.

Mitchell has a wonderfully subtle and witty style of writing. It's sprinkled with lines like, "I sat for a while longer sipping water from my canteen and chewing a ration bar, the flavour of which, as usual, hovered just outside the range of identification," or "a level head is a fine asset on the battlefield, but not when it's been shaped like that by a fragment of shrapnel." It's not that this more subtle humor disappears from subsequent novels (it doesn't), so much as here it has more room to breathe making the story a delight instead of a groan.

Image credit: Wizards of the Coast

Special Edition Extras

The illustrations for the book were provided by Alex Brock who, while a newer face for Warhammer, has done a lot of work for Magic: the Gathering and other tabletop games. Brock, who once described his style as "old master style oil painting with a dark fantasy twinge," gives us an almost monochromatic style accentuated by a very muted gold tone. It's a striking style that I felt matched the book terrifically, with only the tiniest of missteps (there's a scene drawn towards the end of the story showing Cain triumphant with his Commissar's cap, but he'd lost the cap earlier during a wall collapse when underground).

While Mitchell has big shoes to fill following Robert Rath's annotation spree in The Infinite and the Divine (review), he packs a lot of insight into his 130 footnotes. Since Mitchell's Cain stories already use frequent annotations (representing the remarks of Amberly Vail), the reader very quickly gets accustomed to navigating two different sets of annotations based on the color of the ink.

Like previous authors Dan Abnett, Chris Wraight, and Rath, Mitchell takes the opportunity to both pull the curtain back on the writing process for the book as well as hold forth on other topics of interest to the reader. These include:

  • How Jurgen's pornography addiction became the series' first running gag (#44)
  • The value of briefing scenes as stealth exposition (#72)
  • Doing the work to set up the reveal of a mystery (#98)
  • The character development of Cain and other primary (and secondary) characters
  • And perhaps most candidly, how Cain was influenced by Mitchell's own struggles with autism (#47)

There's even one instance (note #68) where Mitchell takes the opportunity to correct something the original typesetter got wrong with the footnotes, likely making this the first time this 'corrected' text has seen print. In addition, Mitchell offers both an introduction and an afterword (even if the former is a bit abbreviated).

Final Thoughts

We're now six books in to the Illustrated and Annotated Series releases, and every one of them has been exceptional. They're some of the best stories in all of the Black Library's canon, wonderfully decorated and filled with additional insight from the author. All that in a hardcover book with bonus treatments (sprayed edging and ribbon bookmarks) typically reserved for higher-end editions. And all this for USD $40?

Long may it last.

This was a worthy entry in the series, and shows Cain at his very best. Don't let this one pass you by.

title: [40k] Ruleshammer 11th Edition: Battle-shock
content:
Welcome back to Ruleshammer! In this series we take a detailed look at the rules of key games, but Warhammer 40k in particular. This week I’m covering battle-shock, its causes, and consequences!

The battle-shock rules are spread out throughout the rules for 11th edition, impacting things such as objective control, actions, and even what move types you can do. This guide aims to bring all of those causes and consequences into one handy reference. At the end of this article there’s a helpful info-graphic summary!

Battle-shock Rolls 01.07

The battle-shock roll itself is simple enough: It’s a Leadership Roll. You roll 2d6 and compare it to the LD characteristics of the unit you’re making the roll for. If it’s greater than or equal to one of the LD characteristics of the unit (which may vary for units with attached characters) then the roll "succeeds." In the case of a battle-shock roll, this means the unit isn’t battle-shocked.

Note that passing this roll during the battle-shock step of the command phase is the only way for a unit to naturally end being battle-shocked unless a unit has a specific ability that allows that unit to stop being battle-shocked. Passing a battle-shock roll at any other time does not cause a unit to stop being battle-shocked.

Causes of Battle-shock Tests

There are several triggers for needing to take a battle-shock test.

Being Battle-shocked Already

This is actually a small but meaningful change in 11th edition that could be wrongly dismissed as not doing anything, but remember that there are ways to be battle-shocked that aren’t being at or below half strength. If an enemy unit has used an ability to make a unit battle-shocked, it could still have its full starting strength on the battlefield but have to take a test at this point regardless.

Also note that removing a unit from the battlefield into reserves or embarking a unit does not remove battle-shock:

Reposition Units 20.02

When they are removed from the battlefield, any rules that are affecting such units for a specified duration or under specific circumstances continue to affect them while that duration and/or those circumstances apply.

Example: … but a unit that was battle-shocked when removed from the battlefield would still be battle-shocked if it makes an ingress move in the same turn.

And you still need to make a battle-shock test for units not on the battlefield:

Not on the Battlefield 01.02.04

… the controlling player must make battle-shock tests for units that are not on the battlefield in their Command Phase if they are battle-shocked, or if they are below half strength.

Being at or Below Half Strength

This brings us neatly onto probably the most likely reason for a unit to start being battle-shocked: Being at or below half strength. This concept has had some subtle changes to be aware of in 11th edition. For the most part it’s still based on how many models there were in the unit at the start of the battle; this defines the unit's “starting strength.” However, if the starting strength of the unit was 1, then rather than using its number of models for this check it depends on the model’s remaining wounds.

Starting Strength and Attached Units

The starting strength of an attached unit is just the number of models in the unit, including the attached ones, at the start of the first battle round (not its number of models during mustering your army, so units that can split up during deployment do not start the battle at half strength). This does not change in 11th regardless of if all the models in the bodyguard unit are destroyed.

19.01.01 Some units have rules stating that when the bodyguard unit in an attached unit is destroyed, leader/support units that were attached to them become separate units with their original starting strength.

When the bodyguard unit in an attached unit affected by such a rule is destroyed, all of those leader/support units remain a single unit for all rules purposes.

This rule is essentially saying to ignore any old rules that say they revert to their old starting strength; they carry on as they were as if it was one big happy unit, that is mostly dead now. So your leaders/support models will still need to take battle-shock tests in this situation, as the unit would most definitely be below half strength.

Note that if the battle-shock test is being made during the battle-shock step of the Command Phase, you usually only need to make a single test regardless of if one or both of these conditions apply.

08.03.01 Multiple Battle-shock Rolls

In the battle-shock step (08.03), unless otherwise stated, no more than one battle-shock test roll can be made by each unit. If for any reason a unit must make a battle-shock roll in this step before one it is required to make for being battle-shocked or at or below half-strength, that unit does not also have to make a battle-shock roll for being battle-shocked or at or below half-strength.

So if anything causes a battle-shock test during this step, that’s the only one you have to make. Bear in mind that you can't choose to avoid enemy abilities here, if a test is required by an ability such as the Psychomancer's Nightmare Shroud.

In the Battle-Shock step of your opponent’s Command phase, if an enemy unit that is below its Starting Strength is within 6" of this model, that enemy unit must take a battle-shock test, subtracting 1 from the test when it does so.

Then this is the test you need to make, even if the unit needed to make one for the core rules reasons. You can't avoid the debuff from this aura by choosing the take one of the "normal" battle-shock tests.

That covers the typical causes; from here we begin to venture into the scatter shot of battle-shock causes that are spread through the core rules.

Making a Desperate Escape Fall Back Move 18.04

Falling back has two modes in 11th edition: Ordered Retreat and Desperate Escape. You’ll see Order Retreat come up again later on in this guide, but Desperate Escape really lives up to its name. Not only does this move require hazard rolls for every model, it also causes the unit the need to take a battle-shock test if it’s not already battle-shocked.

Choosing to gain MOBILE for a move with a model that has the SUPER HEAVY WALKER ability

This is one of the odder ones because whilst there are some automatic battle-shock causes that bypass the leadership roll, this cause requires a roll that isn’t a battle-shock test.

SUPER HEAVY WALKER 24.35

Before moving that unit, you can select for all models in that unit to have the MOBILE keyword until that move ends. If you do, when that move ends, roll one D6: on a 1, that unit is battle-shocked.

Just a straight D6 roll with a 1 in 6 chance of causing the model to become battle-shocked.

Unit Abilities

Plenty of units have abilities that can cause or require battle-shock tests to be made. The T'au Piranha, for example, has its Drone Harassment Tactics ability:

At the end of your Movement phase, select one enemy unit within 12" of this unit; that enemy unit must take a battle-shock test.

These tests are made at the specified time in the ability, not during the command phase or during the battle-shock step, so units will have to take subsequent tests in their next command phase for being battle-shocked.

Automatic Battle-shock Causes (No Tests Made)

There are a few instances in the rules where units can become battle-shocked without any test or roll at all. Those include Combat Disembark Moves 18.04 and Emergency Disembark Moves 18.05. If you make either of these moves, your unit just “is battle-shocked,” so be aware of that.

Core Consequences of Battle-shock

Battle-shock has almost as many consequences as it does causes. This section covers all the core consequences, but factions can and do have rules and abilities that are tied to if units are battle-shocked that would be too numerous to cover here.

Objective Control is modified to “-” 01.07

As its name suggests, the Objective control characteristic determines how much a unit contributes to the control of an objective per model. Having it modified to “-” results in the models in that unit not contributing any amount of control when contesting an objective.

Is there a difference between being modified to “-” or “0”?

No. Some older abilities and rules still reference battle-shock modifying an ability to ‘0’ rather than ‘-’. In 11th edition these are considered one and the same state though, and characteristics modified to either can not be modified again by other rules.

Note that rules that modify a characteristic in this step to a new value of ‘0’, ‘-’, or ‘*’ cannot be modified by other rules (in such cases skip over steps 2-5).

I’d expect more rules to use the ‘-’ term going forward, as ‘0’ implies you can still add modifiers to it in a way that ‘-’ does not.

Controlling player can cannot target such units with Stratagems 01.07

Pretty straight forward one, this; you can’t target them with stratagems. One aspect of this to consider, though, is that this includes the Insane Bravery Stratagem.

First of all, you can’t use this stratagem outside of the command phase, so it can only prevent battle-shock for units that are making their checks in the command phase, but it also can’t be used on units that are already battle-shocked. If the unit became battle-shocked during the previous turn due to an enemy ability or because the unit made a specific move type, then this stratagem can’t be used to succeed on the test that unit needs to make in the subsequent command phase.

Unit is not eligible start an action, and any action it has started cannot be completed 16.01

Important for scoring victory points in many different missions, being battle-shocked causes actions to fail and such units can’t start actions whilst battle-shocked. Pay careful attention to the completion timing of your actions to manage your risk of failing an action if it will take more than a single turn to complete.

Cannot make an Ordered Retreat Fall Back Move 09.07

Whilst you can still fall back, you will be forced to make a Desperate Escape Fall Back move, which I covered above. Ordered Retreat Fall Back moves avoid the hazard rolls and the need to make a battle-shock test, but unlike when making a Desperate Escape Fall Back move, models making an Ordered Retreat Fall Back move can not move through enemy models.

Cannot make Surge Moves 21.01

Closing up the core rules consequences of being battle-shocked is the inability to make surge moves. These are special moves usually triggered by something your opponent has done to your unit, such as the Blood Surge ability of Khorne Berzerkers:

Blood Surge: In your opponent’s Shooting phase, when an enemy unit has shot, if a model in this unit was destroyed as a result of those attacks, this unit can make a surge move of up to D6+2".

Be aware that they do not mention this restriction in the ability themselves; the surge move rules in the core rules restrict them.

Battle-shock Summary

That's all for this weeks Ruleshammer; if you have some questions you think I should cover in the future though please do send them via this form!  Have any other questions or feedback? title: Trench Crusade Warband Focus: Expeditionary Forces of Abyssinia
content:
Welcome everyone to another to another Trench Crusade Warband focus! This week we’re exploring the horn of Africa, as the Expeditionary Forces of Abyssinia try to hold back Mammon’s forces from rolling over the land. We’ll take a look at the Variant rules, unique Battlekit and key units. Let’s get started! 

Editor's Note on the art: We've included artwork we have in our model library for the base New Antioch forces in question, but they're very much not specific models painted for the Expeditionary Forces of Abyssinia. When we get some of those painted, we'll update this piece and republish.

Credit: Raf Cordero

The Lore

Battling the forces of Mammon, the Expeditionary Forces of Abyssinia still pay their tithe, sending their warriors to New Antioch, where they receive cheers and shouts upon arrival.  Hailing mainly from Oromo and Amhara, where the rough terrain has led to many warriors forgoing shoes to battle barefoot. Abyssinia favours a variety of battlefield tactics, but particularly emphasises short-range shooting in formation, allowing the strengths of their detachments to shine. From the mighty Chewa who favour close combat and Shotels, to the Holy Warriors, who are even capable of staving off the spread of the Black Grail, each warrior is honed to achieve their role and defend the Solomonic Throne of Ethiopia.

The Variant

Before we get into things, let’s quickly break down the Variant’s rules: 

  • Abyssinian Healers: You can include up to two Combat Medics, and you can have up to two Misericordias.
  • Chieftain Panoply: No Machine Armour for your Mechanized Heavy Infantry.
  • Faith of Ethiopia: You can’t include any Sniper Priests.
  • Holy Warriors: You can have a single Trench Cleric in your Warband, but also up to two Holy Warriors. Use the regular Trench Cleric rules, but also include the following abilities:

    • Blessed Psalm: As an action that requires no roll, you can play a Blessing Marker from this model and give it to another. 

    • Arise and be Healed! After succeeding a Risky Success Roll, pick a model within 3” of the Holy Warrior, and that model may stand back up and can remove up to D3 Blood Markers and / Infection markers. 
  • Short-Range Marksmanship: Any non-Grenade or non-Heavy ranged weapon fired by a Lieutenant or Yeoman gains +1 if the attack is made at Short Range. 
  • Vanguard Forces: You can take no Trench Moles, but up to 4 Yeomen can have the Flanking ability for 5 Ducats each.
  • Flanking: After regular deployment, but before Infiltrators, you can place a model with this ability touching a battlefield edge and 8” away from any enemy model. However, if a scenario disallows Infiltrators, then this ability cannot be used. 
  • Warrior Nobles: Shock Troopers and Elites may purchase the Chewa ability for 5 Ducats. 
  • Chewa: Add +1 Dice to Melee attack Success Rolls for each other friendly model within 1” of the target. This caps at +2 Dice. 
  • Weapons of Mobile Warfare: You may only take up to three Ranged Weapons with the Heavy Keyword. This does not include Satchel Charges.
Cardinale de Albe. Image: Beezer

Wrapping this all together, we can see that Abyssinia offers a good amount of flexibility in how you approach constructing your warband. Do you want to go for more of a Ranged focus Yeoman build, that is cheap, but can add some fairly reliable firepower, or a Melee build, that focuses on ganging up on targets with your Elites and Shocktroopers through the Chewa ability. Whilst the flexibility is there, I think you’re going to want to lean on the Melee power, not just because of the wider net your Chewa ability can affect (Short-range Marksmanship is just Yeomen and Lieutenant, after all), but because of their unique Battlekit. With that in mind, let’s take a look!

Unique Battlekit

Shotel - 5 Ducats

A cheap 1-Handed weapon that has not only the Critical Keyword but also bypasses the Armour benefits of Shields (but other keywords or special rules still apply). At 5 Ducats, you can’t go wrong with taking this in the early stages against those that like to equip Trench Shields as their only source of Armour, as they are cheaper than Standard Armour.

Holy Water of Lalibela - 3 Ducats, Consumable, Limit: 5 

When a model makes a Success Roll for an Action that can remove Blood or Infection Markers, you can add +1 Dice to that Roll. A really nice consumable to have on your Holy Warriors, and not too expensive at all to have both with this.

Anfarro (Warriors Crown) - 10 Ducats, Chewa & Elite only, Headgear, Limit: 6

This Headgear grants the Negate Fear Keyword, as well as +1 Dice to the Melee Characteristic. Whilst this headgear comes with a few specific restrictions, it is good for your melee bruisers. The Chewa restriction does mean that you’ll be forking out 15 Ducats to get a Shocktrooper with this Headgear, but it can help in the mid-campaign where Ducats are a little more plentiful. For your Elites, it can go nicely if you’re expecting a lot of Fear to crop up.

Tabot - 4 Glory, Holy Warrior only, Limit: 1

Playing into the Blessed Psalm ability of the Holy Warrior, the Tabot is what helps your Holy Warriors generate more Blessing Markers. If you remove Blood or Infection Markers from friendly models with another friendly model, this unit gets a Blessing Marker. Nice and simple, and pairs well with not only Blessed Psalms, but also the cap increase of your Combat Medics.

Key Units

Lieutenant 

New Antioch Lieutenant. Credit: SRM

As with any New Antioch force, your Lieutenant is a key lynchpin in ensuring victory. The lieutenant makes great use of both the Automatic Pistol and Shotel combo, as you will want to get in close with the Pistol to eventually charge, meaning the +1 Dice and Short Range can come in handy, possibly netting you a nice Crit. The Shotel plays nicely into this as well, as with a +2 Dice in melee (and possibly more!), the chance of critting and proccing the Critical keyword is only more likely. 

Suggested starting loadout: 
  • Automatic Pistol
  • Shotel
  • Standard Armour

Holy Warrior 

New Antioch Trench Cleric. Credit: SRM The Holy Warrior is an amazing unit, with two more abilities than their Trench Cleric counterpart whilst still costing the same. With a staggering four abilities, they're able to dish out Blessing Markers around the battlefield as needed, whilst also providing some much-needed healing to a faction that is often very vulnerable to being taken Out of Action from even the smallest of changes to their survival odds. Their damage can catch opponents off guard too, as abilities like Chewa help them punch above their weight, and as we know, more dice mean more Crit chances, so they make use of the Shotel’s Critical Keyword almost as well as the Lieutenant. 

As you progress, you’re going to grab a Tabot for one of your Holy Warriors, so you can start dishing out those Blessing Markers like they’re Tic Tacs. 

Suggested starting loadout: 
  • Automatic Pistol
  • Shotel
  • Holy Water of Lalibela

Combat Medic

In any other New Antioch list, it would be quite rare to see a Combat Medic take an early spot in a list, but with Abyssinia’s unique set of abilities and battlekit, the Combat Medic fits into the playstyle this variants wants to play perfectly. Their natural skills in using Med-Kits pair nicely not only with the Holy Water of Lalibela, but also ensures more consistent proccing of your Holy Warrior’s Tabot ability. Their included Misercordia means they can have some punch in melee, ensuring Downed models stay down, but you need to invest into that to make it more accurate. If your Medic gets promoted, you can grab a Anfarro for them to ensure those strikes hit. 

New Antioch Combat Medic. Credit: SRM

Suggested starting loadout: 

For the most part, the Cmobat Medic comes with almost everything you need, but you may want to add in a Holy Water of Lalibela to get even more reliability in your healing. 

The List

Chew through ya'

Faction: Expeditionary Forces of Abyssinia

Rating: 698 Ducats | 0 Glory

Patron: None

## Elites ##

Lieutenant - 115D

Upgrades & Choices: Chewa

Battlekit: Automatic Pistol, Shotel, Standard Armour

Holy Warrior - 88D

Battlekit: Automatic Pistol, Shotel, Holy Water of Lalibela

Holy Warrior - 88D

Battlekit: Automatic Pistol, Shotel, Holy Water of Lalibela

## Troops ##

Abyssinian Mechanized Infantry - 120D

Battlekit: Heavy Shotgun, Reinforced Armour, Satchel Charge

Yeoman - 65D

Upgrades & Choices: Flanking

Battlekit: Flamethrower

Yeoman - 65D

Upgrades & Choices: Flanking

Battlekit: Flamethrower

Combat Medic - 90D

Battlekit: Misericordia, Gas Mask, Holy Water of Lalibela, Medi-Kit, Musical Instrument, Frag Grenades, Standard Armour

Shocktrooper - 67D

Upgrades & Choices: Chewa

Battlekit: Shotel, Shotel, Frag Grenades

For this list, it’s nice and simple and combines a couple of core aspects of New Antioch, with the added uniqueness of Abyssinia. At the NA core, we have an Abyssinian Mechanized Infantry, with the staple Heavy Shotgun and Satchel Charge, as well as two Yeoman with flamethrowers. Whilst they can’t infiltrate in the usual sense, they can still use flanking, which is better than nothing. For the Abyssinian flavour, we have all three Elites equipped with Automatic Pistols and Shotels, ensuring we make the most out of each activation. A double Shocktrooper is in there to get into the thick of things, and a double Shotel is no laughing matter for shielded opponents. Lastly, we have our Combat Medic, who supports the Warriors, and has the potential for an early promotion.

Final Thoughts

So there we have it! The Expeditionary Forces of Abyssinia take some core aspects of New Antioch frame and play around with this core nicely, relying on positioning and racking up positive modifiers to punch up, along with the Blessing Marker and healing meta game. If you’re looking for a flexible variant that requires you to move many levers at the same time, then certainly take a look at Abyssinia.

title: Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch Brings Slavic & Balkan Folklore to Life in a New Fantasy TTRPG Setting
content:
Eren Chronicles has launched Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch, a new tabletop role-playing game setting inspired by Slavic and Balkan folklore, on Kickstarter. The campaign, which went live on Tuesday, has already surpassed $120,000 in funding within its first day, making it one of the most notable Dungeons & Dragons 5e campaigns of the year.

Zamanora transports players and Dungeon Masters into a world of rural communities, dark forests, and vengeful witches. The setting is designed to support both Wizards of the Coast’s Dungeons & Dragons 5e and 2024 editions, as well as Legend In The Mist, the rustic fantasy RPG from Son of Oak Game Studio that was recently voted the Most Anticipated TTRPG of 2025.

The Zamanora setting draws heavily from Slavic and Balkan folklore, offering players a chance to explore a world where cautionary tales come to life. Players can create characters from fantastical local creatures such as the mischievous Chorts and the spectral Huants. The setting also introduces unique subclasses, including the Bogatyr fighter, Guslar bard, and Hearth-domain cleric, allowing for thematic storytelling deeply tied to the region’s traditions.

Two new magic systems are introduced in Zamanora: Poppet Magic, a manipulative form of spellcasting, and Ceremonial Magic, which enables non-casters to perform magical rituals. These systems provide fresh ways for players to engage with the game world.

The setting features a variety of mythical creatures familiar to fans of Slavic and Balkan folklore, such as the leshy, baba yaga, and kikimora. These beings are joined by a host of other monsters, each accompanied by detailed descriptions and lore.

The Zamanora Kickstarter offers a range of rewards for backers, from digital PDFs to deluxe collector’s editions. Pledge tiers include options for digital content, physical books, and various accessories. The Core, Deluxe, and Collector’s Boxes include items such as dice, a GMless adventure deck, Baba Yaga miniatures, a DM screen, a monster deck, an illustrated slipcase, and a hand-knitted plushie.

A free demo of the Zamanora setting is available for download on the Kickstarter page, allowing potential backers to explore the world before committing to a pledge.

For more information or to support the project, visit the Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch Kickstarter page.

title: New Reinforcements Arrive in Infinity: PanOceania, Yu Jing, Shindenbutai, and Nomads Expand Their Forces
content:
Corvus Belli has introduced a series of new units and expansion packs for its tabletop game, Infinity, bringing additional options to the PanOceania, Yu Jing, and Shindenbutai factions, while also adding the Nomads to the mix.

Kestrel Expansion Pack Beta: PanOceania’s Colonial Forces

The Kestrel Colonial Force is featured in this expansion, showcasing PanOceania’s adaptability in addressing the challenges of space colonization. As a leading power in the Human Sphere, PanOceania leverages its resources to maintain its position, and the Kestrel forces exemplify this approach. Equipped with advanced technology, these units are designed to uphold PanOceania’s strategic interests.

White Banner Expansion Pack Beta: Yu Jing’s Strategic Elite

Yu Jing, often regarded as one of the top powers in the Human Sphere, continues to strengthen its military capabilities with the White Banner Army. This force has demonstrated its effectiveness in conflicts such as the struggle over Svalarheima. Combining cultural heritage with modern technology, the White Banner Army represents Yu Jing’s commitment to achieving its goals through disciplined and strategic action.

Shindenbutai Expansion Pack Beta: Tradition Meets Innovation

On the distant planet of Shinju, the Shindenbutai serve as the military arm of Greater Independent Japan. This force blends traditional samurai values with advanced technology, creating a unique and versatile unit. Tasked with protecting Japanese interests in Shinju’s challenging environment, the Shindenbutai offer players a distinctive option for their armies.

Yu Jing Action Pack and PanOceania Support Pack

The Yu Jing Action Pack provides players with additional units to enhance their armies, reflecting the faction’s combination of cultural depth and technological advancement. Meanwhile, the PanOceania Support Pack introduces specialized units such as the Trauma-Docs and Machinists, which focus on medical support and technical maintenance to keep PanOceanian forces operational.

JSA Support Pack: The Auxiliary Regiment

The Japanese Secessionist Army (JSA) gains new support options with the Tokusetsu Butai, or Auxiliary Regiment. This unit provides essential medical and technical services, ensuring that the JSA’s front-line forces remain effective. The pack highlights the JSA’s emphasis on a balanced approach to warfare, where support units play a critical role.

Nomads Action Pack: A Faction of Free Spirits

The Nomads, known for their independent and unconventional nature, join the battlefield with their own Action Pack. Originating from three massive spaceships that travel the Human Sphere, the Nomads challenge established norms and offer a unique playstyle. Their focus on creativity and adaptability makes them an appealing choice for players seeking a different approach to the game.

content:

title: The Throne of Thorns II for Ruins of Symbaroum 5E Announced: A Darker, More Epic Chapter Awaits
content:
Free League Publishing has announced The Throne of Thorns II, the latest addition to the Ruins of Symbaroum 5th Edition-compatible game line. This new installment continues the epic six-part campaign set in the world of Symbaroum, with pre-orders now available on Free League’s webshop. Those who pre-order will gain access to an alpha-PDF shortly after purchase via DriveThruRPG.

Scheduled for release in June 2025, The Throne of Thorns II is a 230+ page hardcover book that adapts the third and fourth episodes of the Throne of Thorns chronicle for the 5E ruleset. The campaign is designed for characters of 10th to 14th level and is set against a backdrop of escalating tension and danger. The capital city of Yndaros is in chaos as preparations for a royal wedding unfold, while deadly conspiracies threaten to plunge the Davokar region into war. At the same time, a critical wilderness expedition promises to reshape Ambrian history.

The book includes two full-length adventures, The Darkest Star and Mother of Darkness, which form the mid-section and turning point of the Throne of Thorns campaign. It features nearly 20 color maps detailing various locations, such as towns, forests, and ruins, as well as over 60 stat blocks for non-player characters, including monsters, allies, adversaries, and notable individuals. Additionally, the book provides a collection of handouts to enhance gameplay, offering important information for social challenges and problem-solving.

The Throne of Thorns II requires access to the Ruins of Symbaroum Core Setting books—Player’s Guide, Game Master’s Guide, and Bestiary—to fully utilize its content. Fans of the series can now pre-order the book and gain early access to the alpha-PDF, allowing them to prepare for the adventures ahead of the official release.

title: Vesta Mandate: A Competitive Political Thriller TTRPG Launches on Kickstarter
content:
Storygames Chicago has launched Vesta Mandate, a hard sci-fi political intrigue tabletop roleplaying game, on Kickstarter. The campaign will conclude on March 22, offering backers the opportunity to secure the game in either digital or premium hardcover formats.

Set on Vesta Station, a critical hub between Earth and the Outer Rim of the solar system, Vesta Mandate immerses players in a tense political landscape. A century ago, revolutionaries overthrew the Corporation’s control of the station, but now the Vesta Accords are expiring, and the Corporation is returning with threats of force. As members of the Station’s interim government, players take on the roles of ambitious politicians, each with their own vision for the future. Through scheming, negotiation, and betrayal, they must navigate a web of alliances, secrets, and crises to shape the fate of the colony.

Vesta Mandate is a Powered by the Apocalypse (PbtA) storygame enhanced with mechanics and procedures that introduce competitive elements, transforming it into a political drama. Drawing inspiration from games like Pasión de las Pasiones, Carved from Brindlewood, Blades in the Dark, and The Last Caravan, as well as media such as The Expanse, Andor, Silo, and A Memory Called Empire, the game delivers a compelling mix of hard sci-fi and political intrigue.

Designed for 3-5 players, Vesta Mandate can be played as a one-shot or a long-term campaign. Players assume the roles of cunning politicians, each with a Hidden Agenda—a secret plan that evolves into a large-scale coup or power grab. Balancing cooperation and betrayal, players must navigate Secrets, Bonds, and Schisms while responding to escalating crises that threaten the station’s survival.

The game introduces several innovative mechanics to enhance its political drama. Hidden Agendas allow players to co-create secret schemes with the GM, which grow into game-changing power plays. Each character has a scandalous past, known as Secrets, created by other players, which can be used as blackmail. Relationships are central to the game, with Bonds representing alliances and Schisms reflecting conflicts that can escalate into full-blown disputes.

The game uses PbtA-style Moves to resolve tense moments. Players roll two six-sided dice (2d6) and add bonuses based on narrative questions, a mechanic inspired by Pasión de las Pasiones. High-stakes Machinations allow players to burn Bonds for dramatic, game-altering effects.

The game includes five ready-to-run modules, known as Crises, such as Neural Poisoning, Corporate Espionage, and Water Riots. These modules are designed for minimal GM preparation and can be played individually or as part of a larger campaign. Additional Crises are planned as stretch goals.

Backers can choose from a variety of reward tiers, starting at $7 for a digital PDF of the game. Higher tiers include a premium hardcover zine, illustrated by Tony Tran, and a discounted bundle with City of Blood and Plaster, Storygames Chicago’s previous ZineQuest project set in Gilded Age Chicago.

title: Factions Core Rulebook Now Available for Pre-Order
content:
Modiphius Entertainment has announced the pre-order availability of the Fallout: Factions Core Ruleboo. This new hardback rulebook aims to enhance the Fallout: Factions miniature skirmish game, offering players the tools to create campaigns set anywhere in the post-apocalyptic Wasteland.

The Core Rulebook builds on the foundation laid by the Battle for Nuka-World starter set, which featured three raider gangs from Fallout 4’s popular DLC. The new book expands the game’s scope by introducing four additional factions: the Brotherhood of Steel, super mutants, survivors, and raiders. The 112-page, full-color hardcover provides comprehensive rules, campaign systems, and faction-specific content to deepen the gameplay experience.

Priced at £30 / $37, the Core Rulebook will be available for purchase through the Modiphius webstore and local gaming stores in early summer 2025. It is designed to work alongside the Battle for Nuka-World starter set or the upcoming Tokens and Terrain Pack 1, offering players a complete toolkit for creating their own stories in the Wasteland.

The Core Rulebook includes an introduction to wargaming, core rules for fast-paced skirmish gameplay, and an in-depth scenario system to keep each game unique. The Story Phase section allows players to develop their crew, achieve legendary status, or face the consequences of failure. Faction lists provide detailed profiles for each group, including weapons, perks, and legendary characters.

One of the key features of the new rulebook is its flexibility. While the Battle for Nuka-World starter set focused on a specific area, the Core Rulebook allows players to set their campaigns anywhere in the Wasteland. New mechanics, such as Hazards and Facilities, enable crews to customize their Home Turfs, while Objectives and Hazards replace specific scenarios, creating countless combinations for varied gameplay.

Players can also hire new Legends of the Wasteland, upgrade weapons, purchase chems, and unlock perks for their crew. The updated Story Phase ensures campaigns are more expansive and interconnected, offering greater opportunities for storytelling and strategic decision-making.

title: Wrath of the Wyvern: A Dark Fantasy Solo TTRPG Launches on Kickstarter
content:
A new dark fantasy solo tabletop role-playing game, Wrath of the Wyvern, has launched on Kickstarter. Set in the Umbral Highlands, a land where humanity struggles to survive under the threat of monstrous wyverns, the game casts players as a lone hunter tasked with reclaiming the world from these fearsome creatures. Inspired by Scottish Celtic mythology, the game blends exploration, survival, and tactical combat into a solo RPG experience.

Wrath of the Wyvern introduces a Fate Card system, which replaces traditional dice rolls. This system, powered by the Fury Engine, is designed to create fast-paced, strategic, and cinematic encounters. Players navigate an open-world hexcrawl, making decisions that influence the fate of the Highlands. The game emphasizes replayability, with branching storylines and faction dynamics adding depth to each playthrough.

Combat is a central element, utilizing a custom Tarot-sized card deck to manage attacks, defenses, and special abilities. Players spend Stamina Points (SP) to execute actions and must adapt to the unique behaviors of their enemies. Survival mechanics, such as hunger, exhaustion, and changing weather conditions, further enhance the exploration experience.

The Umbral Highlands are a perilous and richly detailed world. Players will encounter legendary monsters from Scottish folklore, including the Wulver, Ghillie Dhu, and Kelpie, as well as the game’s primary antagonists: the Sons of Rivesk, ancient and formidable wyverns. Each wyvern battle is a multi-phase event, requiring careful planning and strategy.

In addition to hunting wyverns, players can rebuild Crag Keep, the ruined fortress of the Skyfire Order, and recruit allies to aid in their quest. The game also features arcane powers and legendary weapons, offering players opportunities to wield powerful magic and craft unique tools.

Backers of Wrath of the Wyvern will receive a premium package that includes a 140+ page hardcover rulebook, a massive hexcrawl map of the Umbral Highlands, a Wyvern Showdown battlemap, a hero miniature, and access to the Isle of Skye expansion. The game will be available in English, Spanish, Italian, and French, with each translation handled by a native speaker.

The campaign will run until April 3, giving potential backers 28 days to pledge their support.

title: This Monty Python-esque comedy RPG lets you improv as a band of incompetent and dangerously powerful wizards
content:
Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is a new tabletop roleplaying game that allows players to become powerful and incompetent spellcasters.

The upcoming roleplaying game sees any number of players collaborating together to tell a story about a band of chaotic wizards. Similarly to the likes of absurdist, fantastical comedy such as the works of iconic British group Monty Python, alongside the likes of The Mighty Boosh and What We Do in the Shadows, Hello Wizard I have a Problem is all about rapid scenes infused by the strange and unexpected.

Unlike many other tabletop RPGs, Hello Wizard sees its players taking turns to take on the roles of player character and games master. Each scene in Hello Wizard has a single player take the spotlight as their spellcaster, with the goal of impressing their fellow sorcerers with their magic. The active player describes what spells their wizard casts, with the other players acting collectively as a GM and deciding how these spells can go wrong.

Players will use a Problem Generator included in the fantasy RPG’s rulebook as inspiration for what could go wrong with the wizards’ spells, with the book capable of making over “200,000” prompts for possible disastrous outcomes. Once every player has had the opportunity to step into the spellcasting spotlight at least a few times, the game ends and players tally up their ‘points’ - which are decided by a loose improv system - and determine who is the most impressive wizard.

The rules system for Hello Wizard is very straightforward and intended to be easy for players to learn. Setup for the tabletop RPG is also designed to be quick and easy, with players expected to start in little time. The rulebook for the game will contain advice and optional rules players can use to augment their playthroughs too.

Hello Wizard I have a Problem was created by Sam Armstrong, a tabletop RPG designer who has previously made titles such as All Bastard - a fantasy TRPG in which players take the roles of either a band of bragging heroes or the bastards they defeated - and horror roleplaying game Slasher. The artwork for the game was created by illustrator Evlyn Moreau, who has previously worked on RPGs like Liminal High School.

The crowdfunding campaign for Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is on Kickstarter until later this afternoon, with the title potentially being made available on Armstrong’s Itch.io page. A pledge of £8 ($10) will get backers a physical copy of the game in June, alternatively a PDF version is available for £4 ($5).

title: Re-enact Greta Gerwig’s Little Women with this coming-of-age tabletop RPG
content:
New tabletop roleplaying game, Castles in the Air, will enable players to re-enact their favourite coming-of-age stories.

Castles in the Air was inspired by the likes of classic coming-of-age period dramas such as Little Women by Louisa May Alcott - which was adapted into a 2019 film directed by Greta Gerwig and starring Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Florence Pugh, Laura Dern and Timothee Chalamet - and Anne of Green Gables by Lucy Maud Montgomery, which was adapted into a televisions series in 2017 by Netflix.

The upcoming roleplaying game will see players’ characters grow up together from children to adults during the historical era known as the Gilded Age, which took place in the USA from the 1870s to the 1890s and saw an increase in industrialisation, economic growth and migration to the US. Castles in the Air is a collaborative storytelling game in which players construct narratives that centre around the wonders and fears of childhood, before tackling the joys and hardships of adulthood.

Players begin the tabletop RPG as a tight-knit group of children, all of whom have great expectations of their futures and much quieter current lives. In this phase of the story, players develop a shared childhood together by doing the things rural and financially supported kids did during that era: like playing in their local farmlands, swimming in the lakes and watching the stars.

As the player characters grow up, they’ll begin exploring other feelings and ideas that come with age. Characters in the group might develop a crush on someone or form a heated rivalry with one of the other local children. All the while, the player group will grow up together, before eventually reaching adulthood and potentially finding themselves drifting apart as life takes them in different directions - perhaps to only meet once again.

Players will be able to create their characters in Castles in the Air by choosing from a variety of character roles inspired by classic archetypes, such as the troublesome scamp, studious bookworm or spoiled princess. Add onto this a dream, childhood relationships, a family background and a bosom enemy, and players can even create their favourite characters from the likes of Little Women or Anne of Green Gables.

Castles in the Air was designed and written by Melia Carraway, with contributions from co-created by the co-founders of the RPG’s publisher, Storybrewer’s Roleplaying, Vee Hendro and Hayley Gordon, who also co-designed Good Society: a tabletop RPG inspired by the works of Jane Austen.

The crowdfunding campaign for Castles in the Air is on Kickstarter until June 9th, with a pledge of AU$ 99 (£52/$77) getting backers a physical copy of the game in March 2025. Alternatively, players can get a digital version for a pledge of AU$ 34 (£18/$26).

title: Freak War throws Exploding Kittens and Pokémon into a blender for a trading card game you can play at parties
content:
Take the evolving monsters of Pokémon, cross them with the fast-playing chaos of party game hit Exploding Kittens and you end up with something that looks a lot like Freak War, a new party-game TCG that wants to offer the fun battles of trading card games without the effort of learning lots of rules or building a deck.

Freak War is the creation of Nate Galbraith, aka cartoonist sketchnate, who was inspired after watching kids trying to have Pokémon battles using Uno cards, before suggesting they play classic playing card game War (which you might also know as Battle) instead. The result was a mixture of all three, with Galbraith adding a collection of strange creatures to the cards.

Unlike the head-to-head battles of Pokémon, Freak War can be played with up to four (or more) players, who can simply split the shuffled deck between them to play - though there is the option to build your own custom decks if you really want to.

Everyone plays a creature at the same time, with the highest attack level winning the battle. Like Exploding Kittens, the many cards can also introduce various effects that shake things up, including the power to evolve into bigger creatures - Pokémon-style - and equip modifiers to your own or opponent’s cards to boost or reduce their strength.

Whether the players choose a card from their hand or simply flip the top of their deck depends on the mode they’re playing: the more chaotic War, or the more strategic Battle. Both modes can be modified further by King of the Hill and team rules.

If two players draw in attack level, they both discard a card before facing off by playing another creature. The overall winner takes all the cards played and adds them to their win pile, which are reshuffled into the player’s deck - the person who manages to claim all the cards from their opponents, wins.

The weird and wonderful creatures on the cards have a bit of lore behind them, having been created by the emergence of a second sun that mutated familiar animals like rabbits, foxes and fish into muscly fishpeople, a time-travelling tiger, a partying platypus, a dog with a goldfish bowl for a head, a sad bee and a Man Cat that appears to basically be a bloke in a cat costume, among others.

Modifier cards, meanwhile, range from a Super Sword (and a Super Duper Sword) to the power to swap cards with a rival, cancel a modifier or flip coins for the chance of a power boost. Some of the creature effects get playfully meta in the way you’d expect for a party game too, with the scrap-loving Fly Guy gaining power if there’s uneaten food near the players.

As someone who is admittedly tired of many copy-paste or just downright gross party games (looking at you, double-offending Cards Against Humanity clones), I’m fairly charmed by Galbraith’s goofy creations and the sprinkling of chaotic take-that gameplay in the form of a TCG. (The card layout is quite explicitly inspired by Pokémon cards.) Sure, it’s not going to be for everyone, but as something knowingly silly to fill five minutes with friends and family (especially younger players), it looks like solid, breezy fun for $20 a deck. With a bunch of different packs filled with dozens more creatures from buff penguins to cute-looking snails, I’m pretty intrigued just to see Galbraith’s interpretation of the nonsense of modern Pokémon evolutions, too.

Freak War has already passed its fairly modest crowdfunding goal of $10,000 over on Kickstarter, where its campaign will run until June 13th. The game itself is expected to land with backers next June, just in time to take on holiday.

title: New Blade Runner RPG expansion asks how far you’d go for the Replicant Rebellion
content:
A new expansion for the official Blade Runner tabletop roleplaying game invites you to join the Replicant Rebellion.

Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game is based on the series of films based on Phillip K Dick’s sci-fi novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep.

Blade Runner, the first of these films, was released in 1982 and directed by Ridley Scott. The film sees Harrison Ford play Deckard, a Blade Runner - an officer whose sole purpose is to hunt and eliminate Replicants, or human-looking androids - who is tasked with finding and killing three escaped Replicants. Following on from the original film, Blade Runner 2049 is a sequel directed by Denis Villeneuve and starring Ryan Gosling. In Blade Runner 2049, Gosling stars as K, a Replicant Blade Runner who must follow the trail of a long-escaped Replicant fugitive and investigate the truth behind her death.

Both films take place in the same fictional science fiction universe wherein Replicants were designed and created entirely to fulfil the needs and wants of their human makers. The Blade Runner franchise is known for its cyberpunk aesthetics, as well as grim view of a near-future wherein corporations are able to commit terrible acts without consequence and exploit large swathes of people.

Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game usually has players taking the roles of Blade Runners within the LA police department during the time period between the first and second films. However, rather than fulfilling their duties as Replicant hunting officers, the next expansion for the sci-fi RPG sees players abandoning their post to join the Replicant Underground.

Replicant Rebellion is a new expansion for the Blade Runner RPG that sees players get recruited into the Replicant Underground, a secret organisation whose goal is to ensure the freedom and liberation of Replicants: whatever the cost.

Players will see themselves become members of the movement - running their own independent crew as they carry out a variety of missions on behalf of the Underground. From laying charges for explosives, sabotaging the Replicant trade and smoking out moles, players must be prepared for all manner of tasks. Members of the group might even find themselves stuck between a rock and a hard place, as they balance their personal morality with the operations of the Replicant Underground.

Both the Replicant Rebellion expansion and the Blade Runner roleplaying game were published and created by Free League Publishing, the studio behind other licensed TRPGs such as the Alien Roleplaying Game.

A crowdfunding campaign for Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game - Replicant Rebellion will be launched on Kickstarter on May 28th.

title: City of Six Moons is a board game written in an alien language you’ll need to translate to play - and you’ll never know if you’ve got it quite right
content:
Upcoming board game City of Six Moons is taking difficulty-to-decipher rulebooks to a whole new level by writing all of its rules in an alien language that you’ll have to translate in order to play. The kicker? You’ll never know if you’ve done so correctly.

The single-player title is described by designer Amabel Holland as being both a game about guiding the fortunes of an alien civilisation, and a game designed as if it actually were made by an alien civilisation in real life.

As such, Holland has written the entire rulebook in a language composed of icons, glyphs and symbols, setting a challenge to the player to decipher the language before they can read the rules for the game itself. To work out its secrets, you’ll apparently need to draw on both your own existing cultural assumptions and the acceptance that the culture of the alien civilisation who made it is very different to humanity.

Cheekily, Holland proposes that players will never quite know if they’ve perfectly cracked the code, and she will refuse to answer any questions about the game’s rules. (Well spotted, BoardGameGeek.)

Given all that, we obviously don’t quite know how the game will play, or even how long it'll take to finish, only that it’ll be a solitaire experience with a set of components needed to play the game in the box alongside the rulebook. Presumably those components will either be devoid of language or marked in the same code as the rules, though we also don’t know what game pieces will be included just yet. We have seen the cover artwork at least, which presumably might offer a first clue to decoding the iconographic language.

Holland did confirm over on Bluesky that City of Six Moons will be a “functional, replayable game” for those who do successfully figure out its rules (or enough to play, that is), though deciphering the code is considered a key part of the package - meaning that players might find it a “lesser” experience after they know its secrets. Yet even that permanent change in understanding is part of the overall journey, Holland believes: “That loss is a thing I want you to feel; I want it to linger.”

City of Six Moons is due for release next month from Holland’s own (alongside co-owner Mary Holland) publishing label Hollandspiele. Good luck to anyone preparing to tackle the cryptic puzzle.

title: Alternate cover for Dungeons & Dragons’ Player’s Handbook radiates a wholesome vibe for players who want to D&D and chill
content:
The front cover for the alternate version of the next Dungeons & Dragons Player Handbook has been revealed.

Last week saw the unveiling of the artwork for the front cover of the Player’s Handbook, for the next version of tabletop roleplaying game - Dungeons & Dragons. Featuring depictions of classic characters from the history of the RPG - such as Strongheart the Knight, Elkhorn the Dwarf Warrior and Yolande the Elven Queen - the front cover shows a party of D&D adventurers and heroes preparing to fight against a horde of Kobolds, a classic Dungeons & Dragons enemy, with a friendly golden dragon standing behind them.

The artwork strongly implies that the group is in the midst of a battle, thereby emphasising the action elements of the fantasy roleplaying game over anything else - which is what D&D is largely known for, at least amongst the general public.

By contrast, the artwork for the front cover of the alternate version of the new D&D Player’s Handbook was revealed soon afterwards - showing a much different approach. (Thanks Polygon) Designed for collectors or players who aren’t keen on the appearance of the standard version, the alternative versions of D&D books don’t differ much from their standard counterparts beyond the outside aesthetics and front cover.

The artwork for the cover of the alternate version of the next D&D Player’s Handbook also depicts a party of adventurers, this time in a very different situation from those shown on the front of the standard book. A classic Dungeons & Dragons party - complete with wizard, cleric, fighter and rogue - are shown sharing a pot of tea inside what looks like the inside of a cave. Included within this serene tea party is a golden dragon - somewhat linking things back to the standard cover - who grasps a normal-sized tea cup in one massive paw, with the party’s rogue balancing on part of the dragon’s body above.

This illustration by artist Wylie Beckert, who is also responsible for the front cover of the alternative version of Dungeon & Dragons: Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, certainly gives off a very different vibe to that of the cover for the standard version of the new Player’s Handbook, which was created by Tyler Jacobsen, providing players who prefer a more relaxed and introspective approach to roleplaying with a more suitable option.

The alternate version of the new D&D Player’s Handbook will be available from local game stores from September 3rd, before the wider release of the book on September 17th.

title: Spend another five hours moving three spaces in the new Talisman board game from the studio behind Betrayal at House on the Hill
content:
A new edition of Talisman, the classic adventure board game, is coming from the publisher behind Betrayal at House on the Hill.

Originally released in 1983, Talisman is a board game wherein two to six players compete to acquire the Crown of Command, which is held directly in the centre of the board. The original edition of the title was published by Games Workshop - the company behind the Warhammer and Warhammer 40K series of miniatures games - and designed by Robert Harris. In the game, players choose from a selection of characters inspired by classic fantasy roleplaying game archetypes, before travelling through each ring of the board in order to reach the middle.

The series has changed over the years, with Fantasy Flight Games - the company behind the recent Star Wars Unlimited trading card game - taking over publishing rights in 2008 before releasing a revised version of the Fourth Edition of the title. As players progress through the game, they’ll acquire new equipment, abilities and allies they can use to overcome the various challenges that block them from entering the inner rings of the board. Gaining these advantages can require players to pass a skill check of some kind, with each starting character offering a different array of statistics.

Players may also have to defeat a rogue’s gallery of monsters during the fantasy board game, all for the goal of completing a Talisman quest in order to enter the board’s inner world. Other players may challenge each other through combat, with any losing player being forced to fall back behind the winner. Whichever player reaches the Portal of Power first claims the Crown of Command, which they can use to eliminate all other players and win.

Talisman 5th edition, officially known as Talisman: The Magical Quest Board Game - 5th Edition, will be published by Avalon Hill, a studio that’s best known for releasing the horror board game series Betrayal at House on the Hill. The upcoming board game will have players competing for the iconic Crown of Command by making their way through the board’s rings towards the middle space. Players will be able to choose from 12 different playable characters: including a thief, a monk, a warrior, a ghoul and a sorceress.

This new edition will feature 100 different adventure cards for players to encounter during their journey through the land of Talisman, all of which include illustrations - with the entire board game containing brand new artwork and updated components. The gameplay for 5th edition has been “streamlined” to make it more accessible to less experienced players, with no more details about its gameplay available beyond that.

Talisman: The Magical Quest Board Game - 5th Edition is set to be released on August 1st for a retail price of $60 (£47).

title: Hannibal and Hamilcar bring two out-of-print classic historical wargames back to crowdfunding (Sponsored)
content:
This article is sponsored by Phalanx. Find out more about Hannibal & Hamilcar and back it on Gamefound until May 24th.

Two classic historical board games retelling the clash between Rome and Carthage during the Punic Wars have returned to crowdfunding, giving you another chance to pick up the out-of-print pair of card-driven strategy titles.

The latest Gamefound campaign for Hannibal & Hamilcar brings together designer Mark Simonitch’s acclaimed nineties wargame Hannibal: Rome vs. Carthage, in its new streamlined and revised Classic Edition, with Hamilcar: Silver Edition, designed by Raymond de Maria based on Simonitch and John Rodriguez’s Hannibal companion game Hamilcar: First Punic War, which used similar gameplay mechanics and some of the same components to focus on the naval portion of the conflict.

Both games put a card-driven system at their heart, with each of two players controlling either Rome or Carthage using an asymmetrical deck of strategy cards to command their units around the map, reinforce their armies, sway different regions to their control and trigger historical events based on the period. When armies collide - whether on land or at sea - a separate set of battle cards are used to resolve clashes, requiring players to juggle their political and military ambitions to achieve overall victory.

Hannibal & Hamilcar’s combined re-release in 2018 was named BoardGameGeek’s Best Wargame at the Golden Geeks that year, with the original Hannibal: Rome vs. Carthage taking home the same award and the top prize for Best 2-Player Board Game a decade earlier. The two-in-one title currently sits at a BoardGameGeek user rating of 8.3 out of 10, with over 6,700 reviews, making it the 18th highest-rated wargame on the site at the time of writing. Unlike the collected re-release of Hannibal & Hamilcar, this latest printing sees the two games' newest editions offered as separate boxes.

Publisher Phalanx’s latest crowdfunding campaign for Hannibal & Hamilcar over on Gamefound provides another chance to pick up the out-of-print games - separately, or together in a bundle - along with a new exclusive set of metal miniatures finished in a dark wash to represent the Roman and Carthaginian generals in both titles. The miniatures will only ever be available via the crowdfunder, Phalanx confirmed.

Both games can be had for €80 together or €45 each, with the 26 metal miniatures contained in a €95 wooden storage box illustrated with Hannibal Barca; €160 will get you the full package of both games and the new shiny figures. The re-released games are expected to arrive in August next year, with the Gamefound campaign giving you until May 24th to pledge.
